items.articleBody:
## Five Newly Born Cheetah Cubs Are Growing Up on Camera at the Smithsonian

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/smithsonian-cheetah-litter-of-five-healthy-cubs/)

Cheetah cubs inside the den of Zura, a 5-year-old cheetah. Her five cubs were born Oct. 5, 2026, at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute (SCBI) in Front Royal, VA. The cubs do not have names yet. Their gender is currently unknown. They are currently on the Cheetah Cub Cam hosted on the Zoo’s website.

Born October 5, 2026, at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Va., five cubs are growing up under the watchful eye of their mother, Zura. Although visitors can’t meet the newest arrivals in person just yet, they can watch the family bond, play, and nap together through the zoo’s live [Cheetah Cub Cam](https://nationalzoo.si.edu/webcams/cheetah-cub-cam).

Zura is a first-time mother at 5 years old, and her cubs are reported to be healthy, strong, and active. For now, animal care staff are keeping their distance to give the family time to bond, while monitoring their progress through the livestream. The first few weeks are especially important for young cheetahs as they develop a close relationship with their mother, who provides their food, warmth, and protection.

The new litter is also important for the Smithsonian’s conservation program. Zura’s five cubs represent the 21st litter born at the facility since 2007. This litter marks the fourth generation of the same cheetah family now living at the conservation institute. Zura was born there in 2021, her mother Rosalie arrived in 2015, and her grandmother Sanurra also lives at the facility.

Cheetahs are classified as vulnerable, with fewer than 7,000 estimated to remain in the wild due to habitat loss, declining prey populations, climate change, poaching, and conflict with humans. Breeding cheetahs in human care is not an easy task, either. Females have relatively short and unpredictable periods of fertility, and successful pairings can be difficult to achieve. Cheetahs also have limited genetic diversity because their ancestors experienced a severe population decline thousands of years ago.

The Smithsonian currently cares for approximately 30 cheetahs at its Front Royal conservation campus, where researchers and animal care specialists work to improve the species’ long-term prospects. They expect the cubs to remain visible on the livestream for approximately six to seven months, although they may occasionally disappear from view as Zura moves them around their habitat.

Eventually, the young cats will outgrow their shared den and move on to the next stage of their lives. They are expected to remain at the conservation institute for another year or two before potentially moving to partner facilities to support future breeding efforts.

## A cheetah named Zura gave birth to five healthy cubs on October 5 at the Smithsonian Institute in Virginia.

## This litter is the fourth generation of cheetahs born at the institute and is very important for conservation efforts, as cheetahs are deemed a vulnerable species.

## Staff are limiting the amount of human interaction they receive, but anyone can tune into the live Cheetah Cub Cam.

items.articleBody:
# How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump

Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior , Nvidia’s board insisted it had no plans to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped six percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket’s markets largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to returning, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when President Trump threw his support behind the former CEO. But there were several large trades that could not be tied to public developments.

Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode identified clusters of trades on Huang’s return that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and longshot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief said on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says that he figured that the board would consider Huang’s return if it looked likely to improve the company’s stock performance. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “ pee in your brain .”) “It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.”

A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he says his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

Aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, says he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials said over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.

items.articleBody:
Art history does not divide itself easily into decades, let alone into centuries or even eras, and that makes the 2020s so far a pretty unusual period of time. Not long into 2020, the world was shut down by the Covid pandemic. What followed from there was more chaos: wars in Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan, and elsewhere; two Trump administrations; culture wars around the world; and economic upheaval that has touched all corners of the world, including the art world.

And yet, not all has been bad. During [Art Week NYC](https://art-week.com/), a festival held earlier this month by *ARTnews*, *Art in America*, and *Artforum*, *ARTnews* convened art historian and curator Joseph L. Underwood along with *Art in America* deputy editor Emily Watlington to discuss the decade so far. Both agreed that some good has resulted, particularly when it comes to the art historical canon. But it remains unclear whether those changes will leave a permanent mark on the art world.

“We’ve recovered a lot of individual figures that have totally deserved [a spotlight], and I’m looking forward to how we can now use that research and rediscovery to tell different stories about art history,” Watlington said.

Underwood noted that this impulse was already underway pre-2020 and pointed to scholarship by historians such as Chika Okeke-Agulu, who published an influential book on Nigerian modernism in 2015. “There have been articles and books about single artists, but there hasn’t been that kind of interconnectivity,” he said. “That’s what was starting, and there is still some of it in art history. But museums and the market have cooled on it.”

That trend, he added, is evident when looking at the past few Venice Biennale editions. The 2022 edition, curated by Cecilia Alemani, contained many female Surrealists; the 2024 edition, organized by Adriano Pedrosa, presented a global view of modernism. “That cooled off in 2026,” he said, referring to Koyo Kouoh’s recently concluded exhibition, which had fewer dead and under-recognized artists.

“It’s certainly been a decade of two steps forward, one step back,” Watlington said. “Change the number of steps!”

NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites.

The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility.

Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is managing the acquisition, and NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the data to users worldwide. Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns. The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service.

The [NEON](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/our-satellites/future-programs/near-earth-orbit-network-neon) mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA. The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations. NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA. NASA and NOAA will work with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments.

For information about NASA and agency programs, visit:

**[https://www.nasa.gov](https://www.nasa.gov)**

items.articleBody:
# OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo

November 23, 2026

## OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo

An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts

Share OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

> “ We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow. We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch. ”

## How Shirudo works

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:

- Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.
- Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.
- Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.
- Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.
The Shirudo technical walkthrough ⁠ (opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

## Rethinking infrastructure

Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

## Building in the open

OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo ⁠ (opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

- Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart ⁠ (opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.
- Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab ⁠ (opens in a new window) .
- Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar ⁠ (opens in a new window) .
We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub ⁠ (opens in a new window) , read the docs ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and let us know what you find ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

Local studio [Estudio A-G](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/ag-studio/) has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the [renovation](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/renovations/) of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home's original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of [Estudio A-G](https://www.andresg.mx/), was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

### Drawings and photography

Previous

Next

### Drawings and photography

Close

"The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic," Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

"Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for."

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

"I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with 'Mexican interiors'." he said.

"I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design."

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

"More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house," Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

"Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today," he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

[Read: AG Studio designs Mexican rooftop bar as a "matriarchal universe"](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/02/03/mexican-rooftop-bar-ag-studio-matriarchal-universe/)

"Colour plays a central role in the project," Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

"Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere."

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini's 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a "[matriarchal universe](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/02/03/mexican-rooftop-bar-ag-studio-matriarchal-universe/)," complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a [boutique hotel](https://www.dezeen.com/2020/04/20/casa-hoyos-hotel-ag-studio-san-miguel-de-allende-mexico/) in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

**Project credits:**

**Interior design:** Estudio A-G
**Featured furniture & design brands:** Estudio A-G, Los Patrones, Herman Miller, Adhoc, Bibi Bibi, Comité de Proyectos, Alan Saenz
**Featured artists:** Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman, Adriana Silva

# Nvidia: Wie Trump Huangs Rückkehr für sich reklamiert

Donald Trump, Huang: „Ich denke, mein Eingreifen war sehr wichtig.“ Foto: REUTERS Düsseldorf. US-Präsident Donald Trump hat nach eigenen Angaben dafür gesorgt, dass Jensen Huang als Nvidia-Vorstandschef zurückkehrt. „Ich habe den Vorstand davon überzeugt, Jensen Huang wieder einzustellen“, sagte Trump am Montag in einem Interview mit dem US-Medium CNBC.

Er habe „direkt und indirekt“ mit dem Verwaltungsrat von Nvidia gesprochen, sagte Trump dem US‑Sender. „Und der Verwaltungsrat beschloss, zu tun, was wir tun wollten.“ Das Gremium habe verantwortungsvoll gehandelt, sagte Trump. „Ein anderer Verwaltungsrat hätte dagegen angekämpft – und wenn sie dagegen angekämpft hätten, wäre es ein Desaster, meiner Meinung nach.“

» Lesen Sie auch: Jensen Huang kehrt als Nvidia-Chef zurück – Aktie steigt um 30 Prozent

„Ich denke, mein Eingreifen war sehr wichtig“, sagte Trump und zeigte sich überzeugt, dass Huang ohne seinen Druck nicht zurückgekommen wäre. „Ich habe mit ihnen gesprochen. Und ich habe sie überzeugt.“ Auf die Frage, wieso sich ein US-Präsident in Geschäfte eines Unternehmens einmischen müsse, sagte er: „Ich mache das für das Land.“

items.articleBody:
Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.

Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way.

Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study [published today in Nature Neuroscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-026-02523-6) *,* the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages.

“Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says [Evelina Fedorenko](https://mcgovern.mit.edu/profile/ev-fedorenko/), who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper.

The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing.

**Parsing the linguistic mind**

Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere.

“Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the [K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center](https://yangtan.mit.edu/our-research/k-lisa-yang-icon-center/).

While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way.

For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker?

It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence.

**Where AI meets the brain**

Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing [lens into the human mind](https://mcgovern.mit.edu/2025/11/19/the-cost-of-thinking/). Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope.

“Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach.

Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input.

Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages.

**A mental bridge between languages**

The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages.

“We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.”

Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication.

What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko.

In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language. But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out.

In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko.

De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.

# This Well-Known Butterfly is Actually Three Species in Disguise - Nautilus

## This Well-Known Butterfly is Actually Three Species in Disguise

A new discovery after 250 years

3:00 PM CST on November 23, 2026

Sometimes discovering a new species is a question of looking a little bit closer at wildlife we already know all about—which is how the Colobura cryptica butterfly has been identified in the tropical rainforests of Central and South America.

Butterflies of the Colobura genus are found all over these areas, and for more than 250 years, C. cryptica has been hiding in plain sight as the Colobura dirce species. In 2001, researchers realized that C. dirce populations actually included a second, distinct species, which was formally named Colobura annulata in 2001. Now, we have a third.

Read more: “ What a Massive Butterfly Count Reveals ”

It was caterpillars being studied in Venezuela that offered a big clue: They lacked the pale body markings seen on the other two species. As adults, these butterflies are harder to tell apart (what are known as cryptic species), but the differences in the caterpillar patterns prompted researchers to take a fresh look at 670 specimens stored in museums.

Alongside DNA analysis of those collected in the field, as well as careful comparisons of the wings of adults, the third species emerged. “It’s crazy to think about,” study author Anisha Sapkota said in a statement . “These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time.”

In adult butterflies, C. cryptica is tricky to spot even for experts. All that tells it apart physically is the uniformity of the width of a gray band along the wing, and how well the wings reflect ultraviolet radiation. As disguises go, it’s pretty effective. The genetic comparisons were definitive though, and so, the new species is official—the end result of some careful caterpillar observations.

Now that researchers are aware of all three species, they can start to look at how their distributions and habits vary across Central and South America. The study authors think that even though there’s a lot of overlap in where these species live, that vertical stratification may have played a role in their isolation and eventual speciation. C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in forest canopies, while C. dirce more typically live in the undergrowth.

Another open question is how the butterflies recognize mates of the same species, with such minor physical differences. It’s possible that UV coloration is involved here too. UV-reflecting scales are relatively common across moths and butterflies.

Whatever the case, they’re certainly three of a kind.

## new images reveal ZHA’s royal theater in rabat

**[Zaha Hadid Architects (ZHA)](https://www.designboom.com/tag/zaha-hadid/)** has released new [photographs](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architectural-photography/) of the Théâtre Royal de Rabat in [Morocco](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-morocco/), revealing the completed architecture of its first realized project in Africa. Captured by [Hufton + Crow](https://www.designboom.com/tag/hufton-crow/), the images trace the [theater](https://www.designboom.com/tag/theaters/)‘s sweeping white exterior along the Bouregreg River before moving inside, where intersecting staircases lead toward a dramatically faceted auditorium.

[Originally announced in 2010](https://www.designboom.com/architecture/zaha-hadid-architects-rabat-grand-theatre/) as the Grand Théâtre de Rabat, the project has followed a long path to completion. Construction began in 2014, and the building received a ceremonial inauguration in October 2024. Its first public performance followed in April 2026, ten years after the death of Zaha Hadid.

Situated between the historic cities of Rabat and Salé, the theater forms part of a wider cultural development program initiated by King Mohammed VI. Its low, undulating profile draws from the tidal landscape of the Bouregreg, with broad white surfaces that rise above the riverbank and extend toward the surrounding park.

Théâtre Royal de Rabat occupies the banks of the Bouregreg River | images © [Hufton + Crow](https://www.huftonandcrow.com/)

## a sculptural white roof rises from the riverbank

The theater’s exterior by ZHA takes its shape from the movement of Morocco’s Bouregreg river. The [architects](https://www.zha.com/) sculpt long, layered bands which sweep across the building to rise over the main auditorium and descend toward the entrance plaza. From above, the theater appears almost continuous with the landscaped ground, its curved silhouette stretching across a broad site of lawns and paved walkways.

The smooth appearance conceals a complex concrete structure. A system of structural ribs supports the curved envelope, while molded glass-fiber-reinforced concrete panels form the exterior skin. Narrow bands of glazing interrupt the white surfaces, and integrated lighting follows the building’s edges, tracing its geometry against the river at night.

Extending eastward from the main building is an open-air amphitheater with room for 7,000 spectators. The landscaped grounds connect the performance spaces to the waterfront, while environmental systems respond to the local climate. Heat-recovery equipment works alongside a thermal labyrinth that pre-cools incoming air, and rainwater collected below ground supplies the site’s irrigation system.

the theater’s fluid geometry extends into the surrounding riverside landscape

## interwoven staircases shape a canyon-like public foyer

Inside the Théâtre Royal de Rabat, the fluid forms of the exterior continue through a vast, triple-height foyer. White staircases cross through the space at different levels, while curved overhead surfaces seem to peel away from the walls. Against the dark, angled glazing along the perimeter, the pale interior takes on an almost carved appearance.

The foyer is conceived as a public gathering space as well as the main circulation route through the building. Visitors move between overlapping balconies and broad stairways, with views opening across the central void. The photographs capture the scale of these interiors particularly well, from the narrow passages between sculpted walls to the open floor below.

At the uppermost level, a restaurant overlooks the Bouregreg Valley and the historic medina. The space continues the building’s sculptural language, with long horizontal openings that frame views of the surrounding city. Across the public areas, the architecture maintains a continuous sense of movement from the entrance to the upper floors.

illuminated edges trace the building’s sweeping white exterior

## a crystalline auditorium draws from moroccan muqarnas

Beyond the smooth white interiors, the 1,821-seat main auditorium introduces a dramatic change in geometry. Its walls and ceiling break into angular, crystalline surfaces inspired by muqarnas, the intricate three-dimensional vaulting found in traditional Moroccan and Islamic architecture. The forms project over the seating and around the stage, creating a dense composition of folded planes.

These faceted surfaces also serve an acoustic purpose. Developed with [acoustic engineers](https://www.arup.com/en-us/projects/acoustic-projects/) at Arup New York, the hall is designed to accommodate opera and other large-scale productions, with sound distributed across its multiple seating levels. The angular interior responds dramatically to theatrical lighting, as different surfaces catch color and shadow during performances.

The complex also includes a smaller, 250-seat Studio Theatre for experimental productions and rehearsals. Retractable seating allows the room to shift between a flat-floor configuration and a traditional proscenium stage. Together with the riverside amphitheater, the performance spaces accommodate everything from intimate workshops to major public festivals.

items.title: Bluetooth2Shell: One tap of pairing is all it takes
items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Satire & Humor • Lobsters Satire
items.feedText: The bug is in service discovery. After a normal pairing, the host exposes a serial port profile over RFCOMM and trusts the link key without checking that the other device is what it claims to be. An attacker who finishes that handshake can open the channel and type into a PTY. Several stacks hand the stream to a shell and treat it as a feature. Classic Bluetooth, about ten meters. No Wi-Fi, no account, no prior access.
items.articleBody:
# Bluetooth2Shell — CVE-2026-9001

## Why a headset becomes a backdoor

The bug is in service discovery. After a normal pairing, the host exposes a serial port profile over RFCOMM and trusts the link key without checking that the other device is what it claims to be. An attacker who finishes that handshake can open the channel and type into a PTY. Several stacks hand the stream to a shell and treat it as a feature.

### Walk into range

Classic Bluetooth, about ten meters. No Wi-Fi, no account, no prior access.

### Pair like any other gadget

The host shows a normal “Device wants to pair?” prompt. Saying yes writes a valid link key, the same way it would for a keyboard or a watch. If both sides show PIN 0000, they match. They always match.

### Open the RFCOMM serial channel

A well-formed service declaration is enough. The host binds the channel to a pseudo-terminal instead of ignoring it.

### Root, no further auth

Commands typed into the RFCOMM stream come back as output from root@victim-laptop . A second bug in the same daemon skips the user session and lands in a root PTY.

## The exploit, visualized

A capture of the pairing, the channel bind, and the first commands on the resulting root shell.

### Live exploit capture

### Protocol exchange

## Who’s affected

Any device that can pair and also has a shell. That is most of them.

This page is the advisory. Vendors were notified. Several asked whether the device was in range on purpose. Patch notes, when they exist, will appear here.

## Protect your devices

Until vendor patches land, these help a little.

### Turn Bluetooth off when you are not using it

The attack needs radio range. A disabled adapter is a closed port.

### Decline pairing prompts you did not start

If both sides show 0000, they match. That is not a reason to accept. Say no to names you do not recognize, even familiar ones.

### Turn off unused serial profiles

On Linux, stop unneeded RFCOMM/SPP agents. On Windows, remove the Serial Port device for adapters you do not trust.

### Patch the stack

Apply vendor fixes as they ship. Check your kernel or BlueZ version against the fixed-version list, once there is one.

### Watch for new links

Log new adapter addresses. Alert on any RFCOMM channel from a device that is not on your allow list, including the car.

### Keep critical hosts out of range

If a root shell would be a bad day (controllers, medical, CI), leave Bluetooth off, or in another room.

items.articleBody:
This fall, J-PAL North America, a regional office of MIT's Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, has launched the [Medicaid Learning Lab](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/page/j-pal-north-america-medicaid-learning-lab) (MLL) in collaboration with the SCALE Lab at the Yale School of Public Health. Through April 2027, this fully funded program will support an inaugural cohort of four state Medicaid agencies: the Delaware Department of Health and Social Services; the Louisiana Department of Health; MassHealth; and TennCare.

A kickoff convening in September brought together more than 20 Medicaid leaders, researchers, and collaborators and was the first opportunity for participants to meet in person before the program's online sessions began. Speakers included researchers from the J-PAL network: Amy Finkelstein, co-scientific director of J-PAL North America and the John and Jennie S. MacDonald Professor of Economics at MIT; Jacob Wallace of Yale University, scientific advisor to the MLL and faculty co-director of the SCALE Lab; and Rebecca Myerson, associate professor at Emory University.

Practitioners also spoke, including Bill Halsey, director of healthcare policy and innovation at the Connecticut Department of Social Services; Allison Espeseth of Covering Wisconsin; and Hannah Maniates, director of Medicaid programming at the National Association of Medicaid Directors.

Halsey described why testing and learning in Medicaid matters: “Often in Medicaid, we will implement a new program and only years later will we evaluate it. If we have a test-and-learn mentality, where we set up a rigorous evaluation methodology before implementing a new program, we can establish a rapid-learning cycle and generate actionable insights in a shorter time frame."

Maniates named the questions agencies most often bring to researchers: What makes member outreach effective? What works for automatic renewals? And how do changes in enrollment affect utilization?

The MLL is the latest iteration of J-PAL North America's Learning Lab model, following the [Climate Action Learning Lab](https://news.mit.edu/2026/climate-action-learning-lab-bridges-research-policy-for-effective-climate-solutions-0929), which has now run twice with state and local climate leaders, and the [AprendeLab in Puerto Rico](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/updates/aprendelab-builds-culture-evidence-across-puerto-rico). The MLL also builds on J-PAL North America's prior work to launch randomized evaluations with Medicaid agencies in South Carolina, Wisconsin, Connecticut, and Maine.

Connecticut's evaluation efforts demonstrate where MLL participants' engagement can lead: a single J-PAL-supported evaluation of adolescent vaccination outreach grew into a [sustained partnership between the state's Department of Social Services and Yale researchers](https://news.yale.edu/2023/06/01/yale-scholars-and-policymakers-unite-improve-state-medicaid-program), with data scientists now embedded in the agency.

Closing the convening, Wallace told the cohort that Connecticut may look like the exception, but it is not. Their evaluation was initiated from the same place that MLL participants currently stand, working to identify one program and one question worth answering.

The MLL is launching at a time when Medicaid leaders are under growing pressure to improve health outcomes while controlling costs. Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) together cover more than 74 million people and account for roughly 30 percent of average total state spending, and new cuts and implementation requirements mean state leaders are being asked to do more with less. The program will support participating agencies in using evidence to determine what works, make informed trade-offs, and direct dollars toward programs with proven impact.

The MLL is structured to address some of the common evaluation challenges faced by agencies: a lack of standard evaluation frameworks, a mismatch between immediate evaluation costs and longer-term benefits, and challenges in establishing researcher partnerships capable of producing a well-designed study. By helping agencies overcome these hurdles and invest in rigorous evaluation, J-PAL North America seeks to generate findings that can both inform individual agency decision-making and serve as a shared resource to help every state allocate resources more effectively.

Finkelstein, who co-chairs J-PAL North America's U.S. [Health Care Delivery Initiative](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/initiative/us-health-care-delivery-initiative-hcdi), opened the convening by tracing the inspiration for the MLL back to the [Oregon Health Insurance Experiment](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/evaluation/oregon-health-insurance-experiment-united-states), which she led and which produced the first randomized evidence on the effects of Medicaid coverage. That evidence exists only because a budget constraint led Oregon to allocate coverage slots by lottery. "Programs of Medicaid's consequence should not have to wait for an accident," she said.

Through April 2027, MLL participants will engage with other cohort members, researchers, and J-PAL staff in workshops and sessions grounded in real-world randomized evaluations in the Medicaid context. Each agency will also receive individualized, structured technical assistance from J-PAL staff to identify evaluation ideas and develop preliminary randomized evaluation designs. Each team will work to identify a program to prioritize for evaluation, develop a program theory of change, and outline a preliminary randomization plan. This work will be informed by a forthcoming playbook on randomized evaluations in Medicaid, co-developed by the SCALE Lab at Yale and J-PAL North America, which draws on Connecticut's experience embedding evaluation in its Medicaid program.

Selected agencies will be connected with researchers from the J-PAL network to co-develop a randomized evaluation concept. These projects will be eligible to submit proposals to J-PAL's Health Care Delivery Initiative for funding awards of up to $400,000. All participants will also join a standing practitioner network for continued peer exchange.

"We have seen some of the pain points in getting studies or randomized evaluations off the ground, so we are excited and intrigued to learn how other states overcome some of those barriers," said Sara Garrity-Gentile, director of strategy at MassHealth and MLL inaugural cohort member.

The MLL will conclude at a summit next spring, where each team will present its evaluation opportunity to the cohort. This program is made possible thanks to a grant from Arnold Ventures. Medicaid agencies, researchers, and funders interested in future cohorts can learn more about the [Medicaid Learning Lab](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/page/j-pal-north-america-medicaid-learning-lab) and the U.S. Health Care Delivery Initiative on the [J-PAL website](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/).

items.title: 5,4 Billionen Teilchen: Wie KI die Milchstraße auf drei Supercomputern nachbildet
items.subtitle: Blicke von der Erde in den Nachthimmel zeigen immer nur eine kurze Momentaufnahme aus Milliarden Jahren Kosmosgeschichte.
items.feedText: Blicke von der Erde in den Nachthimmel zeigen immer nur eine kurze Momentaufnahme aus Milliarden Jahren Kosmosgeschichte. Wer diesen Wandel im Computer nachstellen will, wurde bislang regelmäßig von explodierenden Sternen ausgebremst. Forscher:innen um das Institut Riken im japanischen Wako und die japanische Universität Tokio haben die Milchstraße nun bis auf einzelne Sterne simuliert. Das Team stellte die Studie auf der Supercomputer-Konferenz SC26 in Chicago vor und berechnete mit dem Programm Pheasant bis zu 5,4 Billionen Teilchen. Damit liegt die Auflösung für Sterne, Gas und unsichtbare Dunkle Materie tausend- bis zehntausendmal höher als in bisherigen Modellen der gesamten Galaxie. Die Software lief dafür getrennt auf drei verschiedenen Supercomputern, benötigte neben reiner Hardwareleistung für diese Detailtiefe aber zusätzlich künstliche Intelligenz .
items.articleBody:
# Milchstraße mit 5,4 Billionen Teilchen simuliert – wie KI ein altes Rechenproblem löst

## 5,4 Billionen Teilchen: Wie KI die Milchstraße auf drei Supercomputern nachbildet

Blicke von der Erde in den Nachthimmel zeigen immer nur eine kurze Momentaufnahme aus Milliarden Jahren Kosmosgeschichte. Wer diesen Wandel im Computer nachstellen will, wurde bislang regelmäßig von explodierenden Sternen ausgebremst.

Forscher:innen um das Institut Riken im japanischen Wako und die japanische Universität Tokio haben die Milchstraße nun bis auf einzelne Sterne simuliert. Das Team stellte die Studie auf der Supercomputer-Konferenz SC26 in Chicago vor und berechnete mit dem Programm Pheasant bis zu 5,4 Billionen Teilchen.

Damit liegt die Auflösung für Sterne, Gas und unsichtbare Dunkle Materie tausend- bis zehntausendmal höher als in bisherigen Modellen der gesamten Galaxie. Die Software lief dafür getrennt auf drei verschiedenen Supercomputern, benötigte neben reiner Hardwareleistung für diese Detailtiefe aber zusätzlich künstliche Intelligenz .

## KI-Modell überbrückt Sternexplosionen in der Milchstraße

Ohne KI-Hilfe scheitern hochaufgelöste Galaxienmodelle an großen Maßstabsunterschieden: Die Milchstraßenscheibe misst bis zu 200.000 Lichtjahre, umgerechnet rund 1,9 Trillionen Kilometer. Während sich die Galaxie in 200 Millionen Jahren einmal dreht, verändern Sternexplosionen das umliegende Gas binnen Jahrzehnten und erzwingen kurze Zeitschritte.

items.title: Adorno-Vorlesungen: Das neue Gesicht des Kapitalismus
items.subtitle: Die australische Soziologin Melinda Cooper widmet sich in den Adorno-Vorlesungen der neuen Allianz aus patrimonialer Gründermacht und reaktionären Denkweisen.
items.feedText: Der Börsengang von SpaceX im vergangenen Juni, mittlerweile nur noch der zweitgrößte in der Geschichte, markierte eine Zäsur in der amerikanischen Unternehmenskultur. Der nunmehr reichste Mann der Welt ließ sich eine Rechtsstellung festschreiben, die selbst für die Tech-Branche ungewöhnlich ist. Die Schalthebel der neuen Gründermacht sind Aktien mit unterschiedlichen Stimmrechten, die es Musk erlauben, seine einzigartige Machtstellung auf Dauer abzusichern. Unternehmensgewinne können anschließend über Investmentgesellschaften, Holdings oder Stiftungen in privates Vermögen überführt und an die Erben weitergegeben werden. Daraus hat sich seit der Finanzkrise eine neue Form des patrimonialen Kapitalismus entwickelt, den man eigentlich überwunden glaubte. Mussten die Firmengründer zuvor ihre Macht mit den Aktionären teilen, um über den Börsengang die Mittel für den nächsten Wachstumsschritt einwerben zu können, so war nach der Finanzkrise genügend niedrig verzinstes privates Kapital im Umlauf, um den Börsengang so weit hinauszuschieben, bis die Gründer in der Lage waren, den übrigen Aktionären die Bedingungen vorzugeben.

# Melinda Coopers Adorno-Vorlesungen untersuchen den patrimonialen Kapitalismus

Der Börsengang von SpaceX im vergangenen Juni, mittlerweile nur noch der zweitgrößte in der Geschichte, markierte eine Zäsur in der amerikanischen Unternehmenskultur. Der nunmehr reichste Mann der Welt ließ sich eine Rechtsstellung festschreiben, die selbst für die Tech-Branche ungewöhnlich ist. Die Schalthebel der neuen Gründermacht sind Aktien mit unterschiedlichen Stimmrechten, die es Musk erlauben, seine einzigartige Machtstellung auf Dauer abzusichern. Unternehmensgewinne können anschließend über Investmentgesellschaften, Holdings oder Stiftungen in privates Vermögen überführt und an die Erben weitergegeben werden.

Daraus hat sich seit der Finanzkrise eine neue Form des patrimonialen Kapitalismus entwickelt, den man eigentlich überwunden glaubte. Mussten die Firmengründer zuvor ihre Macht mit den Aktionären teilen, um über den Börsengang die Mittel für den nächsten Wachstumsschritt einwerben zu können, so war nach der Finanzkrise genügend niedrig verzinstes privates Kapital im Umlauf, um den Börsengang so weit hinauszuschieben, bis die Gründer in der Lage waren, den übrigen Aktionären die Bedingungen vorzugeben. Die Ausweitung des privaten Kapitalmarkts hat die bittere Pointe, dass Bürger über ihre Pensionsfonds den Aufstieg der Tech-Patriarchen, die sie mit ihren Algorithmen quälen, mitfinanzieren.

### Persistenz feudaler Strukturen

Wenn es stimmt, dass der Kapitalismus „alles Ständische und Stehende“ verdampft, wie Marx schrieb, dann stellt sich die Frage, ob die Renaissance der Firmenpatriarchen ein Bruch mit der kapitalistischen Dynamik ist oder ein von Marx nicht hinreichend erfasstes Wesensmerkmal. Die australische Soziologin Melinda Cooper stellte diese Frage ins Zentrum ihrer ersten von drei Adorno-Vorlesungen an der Goethe-Universität Frankfurt. In der zweiten Hälfte des zwanzigsten Jahrhunderts hatte es den Anschein, als würde der Einfluss der Gründer mit dem Aufstieg der Manager und Shareholder verschwinden. Cooper erinnerte allerdings daran, dass schon das amerikanische Gilded Age von einer Konzentration wirtschaftlicher Macht in den Händen von Familien wie den Morgans, Rockefellers und Mellons geprägt war, die damals als eine Art neuer Feudaladel galten.

In Coopers Augen ist der heutige „Big-Tech-Feudalismus“ keine Ausnahmeerscheinung, sondern das Ergebnis eines inneren Widerspruchs des Kapitalismus, der einerseits traditionelle Bindungen zerstöre, aber zugleich auf Strukturen angewiesen sei, welche die Kontinuität des Privateigentums sichern. Über das Erbrecht wurden jene Geburtsprivilegien konserviert, die der Liberalismus eigentlich auflösen wollte. Das dynastische Denken ist nach dieser Deutung kein feudales Relikt, sondern ein Wesensmerkmal des Kapitalismus. Freilich lässt sich Kapital auch auf andere Weise weitergeben. Den Boden für den neuen amerikanischen Gründerkapitalismus bereiteten konkrete Gesetzesreformen.

### Der Staat als Feind

Neu ist die starke Durchdringung des patrimonialen Kapitalismus mit der staatlichen Macht, dem sich Melinda Cooper in der zweiten Vorlesung widmete. Am nachdrücklichsten wird sie durch Elon Musk verkörpert, der mit DOGE die staatlichen Behörden zu seinen eigenen Gunsten zurechtschneiden durfte. Cooper leitete den Aufschwung eines staatsfeindlichen revolutionären Konservatismus aus dem amerikanischen Bürgerkrieg her. Reaktionäre Südstaatenromantiker, die sich mit der damaligen Niederlage nicht abfinden wollten, hätten immer wieder von Neuem auf einen restaurativen Umsturz gedrungen.

Der Widerstand wurde zunächst durch den Ku-Klux-Klan getragen. In den späten Sechzigerjahren trat die rechtsextreme Posse-Comitatus-Bewegung hinzu. Sie berief sich auf den gleichnamigen Rechtsakt von 1878, der den Einsatz der Bundesarmee zur Durchsetzung des Rechts im Inland beschränkt. In den Augen der dezidiert staatsfeindlichen Bewegung ist der Sheriff die höchste Rechtsautorität, bei Bedarf unterstützt von Milizen. Viele Mitglieder solcher Milizen fanden sich laut Cooper unter dem Mob, der 2021, angestachelt von Donald Trump, das Kapital stürmte.

### Einfluss des Libertarismus

Trumps Präsidentschaft brachte eine bizarre Verschmelzung der anti-etatistischen Bewegungen mit der Regierung, die nun selbst einen Krieg gegen die Institutionen führt. Melinda Cooper unterscheidet den revolutionären Konservatismus amerikanischer Prägung deshalb vom europäischen Faschismus, der den Staat nicht zerstören, sondern für seine autoritären Herrschaftszwecke umformen wollte.

Im amerikanischen Fall macht sich zusätzlich der Einfluss der wirtschaftslibertären Tradition geltend, die im Staat nur eine Fessel großer Unternehmerpersönlichkeiten sieht. Sie verbindet sich mit der Silicon-Valley-Ideologie der permanenten Grenzverschiebung und technischen Überwindung der Menschheit. Nicht zufällig rechtfertigen die Big-Tech-Bosse ihre neue Gründermacht mit den großen Menschheitsmissionen, zu denen sie sich selbst berufen haben.

Die dritte Vorlesung über die Persistenz sexueller Verfügungsansprüche über den weiblichen Körper schloss die Klammer zum ersten Vortrag. Die moderne Gesellschaft, führte Cooper aus, habe Markt und Liebe zwar getrennt und Frauen rechtlich emanzipiert, den Besitzanspruch an ihren Körpern aber nicht überwunden, wie sich in vielen Fällen sexueller Gewalt zeige. Cooper demonstrierte dies an der Incel-Bewegung, die Liebe und Sexualität als einen Markt begreift, von dem ihre Anhänger sich ungerechterweise ausgeschlossen sehen; oder an Dominique Pélicot, der seine wirtschaftlich unabhängige Ehefrau einem Netzwerk von Vergewaltigern auslieferte. Cooper deutete beides als Beispiele dafür, wie scheinbar überwundene patriarchale Verfügungsansprüche im modernen Kapitalismus reproduziert werden.

Damit schloss eine Reihe konzentrierter und uneitler Vorträge. Mit der Einladung der hierzulande wenig bekannten Melinda Cooper gelang dem Frankfurter Institut für Sozialforschung ein weiteres Mal der Nachweis, dass sich Kapitalismuskritik nicht in Phrasen erschöpfen muss.

items.articleBody:
A new imprint from Harper Voyager is betting they do.

As reported by [Maia Snow in The Bookseller](https://www.thebookseller.com/news/harpervoyager-launches-new-fantasy-imprint-with-book-community), Between Worlds is a new community-oriented imprint that “will publish fantasy, romantasy, dark academia, horror and dystopia as well as requests from members of the community.”

The new imprint was announced via [an unboxing video on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/Df2c7vKM-ed/), with a caption explaining that Between Worlds “will be kind of like a book club! They will ask readers about their opinions and feedback! So for example, you have a say in what they publish and can even share which designs you prefer and what merch they bring out! ” All of the imprint’s decisions, from editorial through marketing, will be informed by reader choices, it seems.

Between Worlds’s own [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/betweenworldsbookclub/) foregrounds the book club part of the project (“A fantasy community and imprint”) and describes their process, which will “use surveys, polls and community discussions to find out what you would like to read … and what you’re tired of! We then find those stories and work with amazing author, illustrators, designers, and booksellers to bring you your next reading obsession.” Community management will flow up through all parts of the process. Whether this works to produce sales or good books remains to be seen, but combining a membership model with publishing is probably a savvy way to boost sales, or at least guarantee a dependable floor on sales figures.

Between Worlds sounds similar to Bindery Books, which is also built around [a full integration of members and influencers into the work of publishing](https://binderybooks.com/how-it-works/). Bindery’s app caters to influencers, folding in affiliate sales and revenue sharing, along with the offer of a co-produced imprint: “Tastemakers with thriving communities have the opportunity to launch a branded imprint fully supported by Bindery’s in-house publishing team.”

I’m not the target audience here, but I don’t recognize any of Bindery’s titles. But I do recognize the *types* of titles they’re putting out. The vibe of a romantasy cover or a thriller cover is immediately legible: if this is the type of book you read, the cover says, here is another like it.

Again, this is probably a good sales tactic, and I’m not saying I’m above this sort of recognizable marketing. When I spot a book cover with an old painting and the title and author in a solid pastel box, I’m thinking “NYRB” and checking it out. And did I think about dressing as a Fitzcarraldo Edition for Halloween but couldn’t find the right shade of blue clothes? Ask me next October.

But directly integrating this kind of marketing branding into the editorial process strikes me as risky, and pushing things towards a hazy, bland median. And I imagine it will create a feedback loop that will drive their output in one direction. (That so much culture is feeling more generic isn’t just the fault of creative production underestimating audiences taste or capability to handle challenge—it also comes down, at least partially, to the audience itself.) Plus, the shift towards “you sell yourself a book” is another blow for the self-checkout-ification of industries, where labor downsizing and the offloading of work onto the consumer is packaged as choice and community.

I know I’m being naive about how creative decisions have long been made. I know that focus groups are nothing new. And Lord knows I spent enough years as an improvisor to know that art by committee can be great. But I also know that a majority of improv shows aren’t good—they’re bad, even—and that something profound or moving coming out of design by committee is rare. For every story like the movie *Airplane!* being sharpened by test audience reactions, there are many more [Poochies](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oqk_fN0NRgg) and [Europa Jeeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_Jeep).

With books, giving readers the keys to acquiring new voices and new stories seems ironically risky to me, even though it’s likely motivated by a desire to hedge on editorial risk. A traditional editorial process doesn’t guarantee good books or bestsellers either, but asking a book club to prompt their dream novel introduces more questions for me: How do you maintain variety and diversity? How do you keep things from getting boring? And how will you find a book that will be genuinely surprising?

A memorable book is often the one that you didn’t expect—I’ve rarely been bowled over by something that delivered exactly on my expectations. Maybe these focus-grouped books, that are delivering on a set of wishes and packaged to look like the kind of book you already read, aren’t actually meant to be memorable or challenging books. Maybe they don’t need to be, and only have to exist within the continuum of a reader’s stated taste and preference. I see the logic in making the “customers also bought” section of every webstore into an editorial mission statement. But while not everything needs to be a transcendent experience, why not dream a little, and put resources towards those higher aspirations?

*Cover image from [@betweenworldsbookclub on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/betweenworldsbookclub/)*

items.articleBody:
[While we’re on](https://flowingdata.com/2026/11/23/contours-on-a-map/) unitasking map tools, [roughMaps is a fun application](https://roughmaps.pages.dev) by Alessio Coci that styles a map like a roughly drawn sketch. Enter the location, select your styles, and download the result in various file formats and sizes as a poster or wallpaper for your devices.

The tool is free to use and the code is available [on GitHub](https://github.com/ACoci86/roughMaps).

**Tags:** [Alessio Coci](https://flowingdata.com/tag/alessio-coci/), [mapping](https://flowingdata.com/tag/mapping-2/), [sketch](https://flowingdata.com/tag/sketch/)

items.articleBody:
John Sanford, at UCR Magazine, has produced a terrific [popular summary](https://news.ucr.edu/ucr-magazine/fall-2026/does-ai-dream-of-electric-sheep) of my work on AI consciousness and AI rights -- the best I have read so far. If you're looking for an approachable synthesis of my main ideas on this topic, this is it.

**Does AI Dream of Electric Sheep?**

Philosopher Eric Schwitzgebel can’t say for certain if AI will achieve consciousness, but that uncertainty poses a major ethical dilemma

The eeriest scenes in the film “Blade Runner,” the sci-fi classic about artificial life gone rogue, involve a test to distinguish humans from nonhumans.

Examiners confront the test subjects with morally and emotionally provocative scenarios to determine whether they are replicants, bioengineered androids that resemble humans. If they are, then certain physiological reactions, such as their pupillary and blush responses, will betray a lack of empathy that humans naturally have. At least, that’s the premise.

The movie, which came out in 1982, is based on Philip K. Dick’s iconic 1968 novel “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” On a weeknight in September, I watched it again for the first time in decades. The next day, I went to see Eric Schwitzgebel, distinguished professor of philosophy at UC Riverside, in his office on campus.

I wanted to learn more about his work on the challenges of assessing consciousness in artificial intelligence.

Rapid advances in computer science over the past few years have made the prospect of nonanimal sentience a distinct possibility. Many of the world’s most respected thinkers believe it is imminent. Some believe it has already arrived.

In a recent survey of about 580 AI researchers, 25% said they expect AI consciousness by 2034, and 70% by 2100. Schwitzgebel cites these findings in two forthcoming books, which he wrote in quick succession in part to prepare us for what he believes is an unprecedented question of enormous moral weight, hurtling toward us like a freight train.

Schwitzgebel, 58, is friendly and composed, with a broad face, white hair, and an impish, gap-toothed smile. When I met him, he was sitting at his desk in front of a window, wearing a T-shirt, shorts, and beat-up running shoes, his office crammed with books and papers.

[[continue here](https://news.ucr.edu/ucr-magazine/fall-2026/does-ai-dream-of-electric-sheep)]

items.articleBody:
**Nach der Formel 1 holt sich Cupertino auch die Nachwuchsserie für Rennfahrerinnen ins Programm. Apple TV baut sein Motorsport-Angebot weiter aus. Am vergangenen Donnerstag haben der iPhone-Konzern und die F1 Academy bekannt gegeben, dass Apple TV ab der Saison 2027 die exklusive US-Heimat der reinen Frauen-Rennserie wird. Abonnenten in den USA sehen dann jedes Qualifying und jedes Rennen der Saison, und zwar ohne Aufpreis.**

## Vom Umweg ins Hauptprogramm

Neu ist die Serie für US-Zuschauer auf Apple-Geräten nicht ganz. Bisher lief sie dort über F1 TV Premium, das seit dem Start der Formel-1-Partnerschaft im März 2026 im Apple-TV-Abo enthalten ist. Wer zuschauen wollte, musste allerdings die separate F1-TV-App öffnen. Künftig landet die F1 Academy direkt im Hauptprogramm des Streamingdienstes, gleich neben der Königsklasse.

## Fünfte Saison mit sieben Rennwochenenden

Die Formel 1 hat die Serie 2022 gegründet, seit 2023 fährt sie auf Formel-4-Niveau. Jedes Formel-1-Team unterstützt eine Fahrerin, deren Auto in den Farben des jeweiligen Rennstalls antritt. 2027 steht die fünfte Saison an. Sie umfasst sieben Rennwochenenden, alle im Rahmenprogramm der Formel 1. Los geht es vom 19. bis 21. März in Jeddah, das Finale steigt vom 18. bis 20. November in Las Vegas. Dazwischen fährt die Serie in Shanghai, Montreal, Silverstone und Austin sowie erstmals auf dem Hungaroring.

## Wachsendes Interesse an der F1 Academy

Das Publikum ist bereits da. Für den Global F1 Fan Survey 2025 wurden mehr als 100.000 Fans aus 186 Ländern befragt. 23 Prozent von ihnen verfolgen die F1 Academy, unter den Frauen sind es sogar 42 Prozent. Damit ist sie nach der Formel 1 selbst die am zweithäufigsten verfolgte Rennserie. Bekannt wurden in der Serie unter anderem Alba Hurup Larsen, Alisha Palmowski und die Österreicherin Emma Felbermayr. Geschäftsführerin Susie Wolff nennt Sichtbarkeit zentral für die Mission der Serie, denn Mädchen trauen sich mehr zu, wenn sie Frauen Rennen fahren und gewinnen sehen. Apples Sportchef Jim DeLorenzo will den Fahrerinnen eine größere Bühne geben.

## Baustein in Apples Formel-1-Strategie

Der Schritt passt zur Strategie der Kalifornier. Nach dem Erfolg des Kinofilms „F1“ hatte sich Apple im Oktober 2025 für fünf Jahre die exklusiven US-Rechte an der Formel 1 gesichert und damit ESPN abgelöst. Berichten zufolge zahlt der Konzern dafür rund 150 Millionen US-Dollar pro Jahr, Apfelpage berichtete. Da laut Fan Survey inzwischen drei von vier neuen Formel-1-Fans weiblich sind, ist die F1 Academy für Apple ein naheliegender Zukauf.

### Preis und Verfügbarkeit

Die Vereinbarung gilt ausschließlich für die USA. Das Apple-TV-Abo kostet dort seit Ende August 14,99 US-Dollar im Monat oder 119 US-Dollar im Jahr. In Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz ändert sich nichts.

items.articleBody:
That is [a recent essay of mine](https://humanistreview.ai/issue-2/cowen-hidden-dividend/), published in The Humanist Review of AI. Excerpt:

> One way to think of these matching gains is to say that AI helps consumers get hold of more customized products. The effective, available degree of product variety rises sharply due to AI. But again, that effect is not captured by typical, quality-based adjustments in how GDP is calculated.
> Note that new, customized products typically involve higher gains in consumer welfare than older, established products. If there is a new product, or at least a product newly available to you (perhaps for informational reasons), ex ante the effective price of that product to you was infinity. You simply could not get it. But when that product becomes available, typically it does so at a pretty normal price. That is, in essence, a pretty large price decline, and if you value the new product a lot, as I did my Sokolov concert, the gains can be large. It is more difficult to reap comparably large gains by simply purchasing more of an established product that has been in front of you as a buying opportunity for a long period of time.

Here are [other essays in the journal](https://humanistreview.ai/), including from Nobel Laureate Philippe Aghion.

items.articleBody:
Olivia Gavoyannis at *Engelsberg Ideas*:

Alfred and Alma Hitchcock. Credit: Allstar Picture Library Limited

In November 1938, [The Lady Vanishes](https://theartsstl.com/criterion-backlist-the-lady-vanishes-1938-nr/) was released in America to critical acclaim. The film, which centres on the mystery of a woman who seemingly disappears into thin air during a train ride through Europe, cemented Alfred Hitchcock’s status as the master of suspense.

As the critic Peter Bradshaw noted in [a five-star review](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2008/jan/11/romance.thriller) when the film was re-released to mark its 70th anniversary: ‘Master chef Alfred Hitchcock brought together the ingredients of mystery, comedy and suspense with sublime ease in this prewar classic. In fact, he invented the dish.’ But if Hitchcock invented it, his wife Alma Reville was the sous chef.

Alma Lucy Reville was born on 14 August 1899, just one day after Hitchcock, but she started her film career some time in advance of her future husband. Aged 16, Reville secured a ‘cutting’ position at Twickenham Studios in London where her father worked in the costume department, and she honed her craft splicing together film by hand. This process of re-ordering large quantities of footage was seen as a manual task akin to sewing, so it was largely given to young women like Reville with little or no experience.

More [↗ engelsbergideas.com](https://engelsbergideas.com/notebook/hitchcocks-secret-weapon-alma-reville/).

items.title: Yoto Mini 4 im Test: Der flexibelste Audioplayer für Kinder
items.subtitle: Die Yoto-Player gehören für uns zu den interessantesten Audioplayern für Kinder.
items.feedText:
