items.articleBody:
**In Südaustralien müssen Autofahrer ab 70 Jahren nicht mehr grundsätzlich jährlich zum Arzt, um ihre Fahrtauglichkeit nachzuweisen. Eine Auswertung von Verkehrsdaten zeigt, dass die Zahl der Unfälle mit Personenschaden unter Beteiligung älterer Fahrer nach der Reform gesunken ist. Auch bezogen auf die Zahl der Führerscheininhaber nahm ihre Unfallbeteiligung ab.**

**Adelaide (Australien).** Altersabhängige medizinische Führerscheinkontrollen sollen verhindern, dass Menschen trotz gesundheitlicher Einschränkungen weiter am Straßenverkehr teilnehmen. Ob die regelmäßig vorgeschriebenen Arztbesuche tatsächlich einen zusätzlichen Sicherheitsgewinn bringen, lässt sich anhand von Änderungen solcher Vorschriften untersuchen.

Südaustralien hat seine Regelung zur medizinischen Fahrtauglichkeit in den Jahren 2014 und 2015 geändert. Die zuvor ab einem Alter von 70 Jahren jährlich vorgeschriebene ärztliche Untersuchung wurde abgeschafft und durch eine Selbsteinschätzung für Autofahrer ab 75 Jahren ersetzt, an die sich bei Bedarf eine medizinische Untersuchung anschließt.

### Mehr Senioren besitzen einen Führerschein

Forscher des Centre for Automotive Safety Research (CASR) haben nun die Auswirkungen dieser Reform anhand von Führerschein-, Bevölkerungs- und Unfalldaten aus den Jahren 1997 bis 2023 untersucht. Dazu verglichen sie die Entwicklungen in den Altersgruppen der 18- bis 59-Jährigen, der 60- bis 69-Jährigen und der 70- bis 100-Jährigen. Die Ergebnisse liegen als institutioneller Forschungsbericht vor, für den keine externe Fachbegutachtung dokumentiert ist.

Das Team hatte erwartet, dass ohne obligatorische ärztliche Untersuchungen weniger Menschen mit gesundheitlichen Einschränkungen erkannt werden und dadurch mehr Unfälle passieren. Diese Erwartung bezog sich insbesondere auf Fahrer ab 70 Jahren, für die zuvor die jährliche Untersuchung vorgeschrieben war.

> „Mit zunehmendem Alter entwickeln Menschen mit größerer Wahrscheinlichkeit eine Erkrankung, die ihre Fähigkeit zum sicheren Autofahren beeinträchtigt“, sagt Matthew Baldock, stellvertretender Direktor des CASR.

Die Zahl der älteren Führerscheininhaber ist tatsächlich gewachsen. Im Jahr 2014 hatten in Südaustralien rund 125.000 Menschen ab 70 Jahren einen Führerschein, im Jahr 2023 waren es bereits etwa 200.000. Ein wesentlicher Grund dafür ist die Alterung der Bevölkerung.

### Weniger Unfälle trotz mehr Führerscheininhabern

Anders als erwartet ist die Rate der Aussetzungen von Fahrerlaubnissen aus medizinischen Gründen bei den älteren Autofahrern nach der Reform gestiegen. Zugleich sank sowohl die absolute Zahl der Unfälle mit Personenschaden unter Beteiligung älterer Fahrer als auch deren Zahl pro Führerscheininhaber.

Die Auswertung ergab zudem keine Hinweise darauf, dass nach der Umstellung mehr ältere Fußgänger bei Verkehrsunfällen zu Schaden kamen. Aus den zeitlichen Entwicklungen lässt sich allerdings nicht ableiten, dass die geänderten Vorschriften selbst die Ursache für die gesunkenen Unfallraten waren.

### Ärztliche Prüfungen bleiben bei Bedarf bestehen

Die neue Regelung verzichtet nicht grundsätzlich auf ärztliche Kontrollen der Fahrtauglichkeit. Wer in Südaustralien bereits mit einer relevanten Erkrankung registriert ist, muss weiterhin ein ärztliches Attest vorlegen. Bei Hinweisen auf gesundheitliche Einschränkungen oder Unsicherheit bei der jährlichen Selbsteinschätzung ist ebenfalls eine ärztliche Untersuchung erforderlich.

Die Befunde sprechen somit dafür, dass der Wechsel von pauschalen zu gezielteren medizinischen Kontrollen in Südaustralien nicht mit einer Verschlechterung der Verkehrssicherheit einherging. Ob eine vergleichbare Regelung in anderen Ländern ähnliche Entwicklungen nach sich ziehen würde, lässt sich aus den Daten dagegen nicht unmittelbar ableiten.

**Quellen:**

- Offizielle Studienmitteilung von [Adelaide University](https://adelaide.edu.au/about/news/2026/older-drivers-not-making-the-roads-unsafe/)

items.articleBody:
Timothy Williamson will be the inaugural speaker in a new lecture series accompanying a new journal: *[The Chinese Journal of Philosophy](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?)* (CJP).

Published by Oxford University Press, the CJP is an open-access (including no cost to authors) general philosophy journal.

It is edited by Roger T. Ames (Hawaii), Wei Cheng (Peking), Nicolas De Warren (Penn State), Sebastian Sunday Grève (Peking), and You Zhao (Peking).

The journal is open to submissions “from anyone working in philosophy and on all philosophical topics.” According to its [website](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?),

> the journal aims to represent the multitude of topics and approaches that may fall under the heading of ‘philosophy’ in the world today, with a special focus on philosophical research that has the potential to make different traditions of thought more fruitful for one another.

That is to say, it is not a journal primarily about Chinese philosophy, anymore than the *Canadian Journal of Philosophy* is a journal about Canadian philosophy, or the *Australasian Journal of Philosophy* is about Australasian philosophy. The [note](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/xzqk/cjp/intro.htm), “like these other journals, the *Chinese Journal of Philosophy* originates in a particular region whilst editing and publishing as an international collective, operating in English, and promoting work from around the world.”

CJP is currently open for submissions and plans to begin publishing articles in April.

The launch of the journal includes the start of a new lecture series from the [Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies at Peking University](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/index.htm). Williamson’s inaugural lecture is this Wednesday, and will be delivered in person and [online](https://us06web.zoom.us/j/86727223234).

Learn more about the journal [↗ academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?).

items.articleBody:
*A trained car mechanic who plays 150 BPM trance in a shirt and tie, and checks his tracks by dancing around his room. Meet Davyboi*.

In recent years, trance and its faster, more euphoric relatives have found a new generation of dancers across Europe. Among the DJs who have built a following on the back of that revival is Davyboi, a Munich-based DJ and producer with Polish roots. His sets usually sit between 148 and 155 BPM and draw on trance, eurodance, and hard house in equal measure.

Going out in a city where hard techno dominated, he wanted more melody and uplift than most nights offered, so he began playing the records he wanted to hear himself. That approach, delivered in his trademark shirt and tie, has since taken him to Gotec, Rotterdam Rave, and Into The Woods Festival.

We asked him to introduce himself for Introducing, our series on up-and-coming producers and DJs, many of whom have gone on to much bigger things.

## Who are you?

I’m Davyboi, a DJ and producer. I love fast music, big melodies and dancing just as much as the people in front of me. You’ll usually find me behind the decks wearing a shirt and tie.

## Where are you from?

I’m from Munich, Germany, with Polish roots.

## What do you sound like?

Mostly trance and eurodance, but I also love groove, gabber and makina. It’s fast and energetic, with plenty of melodies and vocals. I want people to dance, sing along and have a good time together.

"Your problems are someone else’s dreams"

## Why should we follow what you’re doing?

If you love dancing and getting a bit carried away with your friends, I think we’ll get along. That’s what I enjoy most about a night out, and it’s the feeling I want to share when I play. I’ve also got plenty of new music on the way that I’m excited for people to hear.

## Which of your tracks sums you up? Why?

“Discotheque,” my collaboration with Mika Heggemann. It’s a good introduction to the energy I like bringing to my sets. When I make music, I always ask myself whether I’d enjoy dancing to it if someone else played it. That’s a big part of why I chose this one.

## What have you got coming out in the near future?

My remix of BUNT.’s “I Need You” is coming, and I’ve been busy working on more tracks. There are a lot of ideas I’m excited about, but I want to give each release a little time before moving on to the next.

[quote align=right text="I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely."]

## Who or what is your biggest influence, and why?

A lot of it comes from being on the dancefloor myself. Some nights really stay with you, especially when a DJ plays something you weren’t expecting, and it completely changes your mood. I still think about those experiences when I’m choosing music. I know how much a good night can mean to someone.

## How did you get into DJing OR producing to begin with?

I was going out a lot in Munich, where hard techno was very present. I enjoyed the energy, but I wanted to hear more melodies and uplifting tracks too. Eventually, I started putting together the kind of music I wanted to hear on a night out. Coming from the crowd still influences how I play today.

## What are three things on your studio shopping list?

A monitor, a height-adjustable desk and [Nexus](https://refx.com/nexus/) to use in [Ableton](https://www.ableton.com/shop/live/?affiliate=F4nlA735). A few things to make working on music a bit more comfortable and give me some new sounds to play with.

### Who or what have you sacrificed for your art?

I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely. It’s more that fitting everything in has become harder. Seeing my friends in Munich takes more planning now that I’m away so often. I still want to make time for them, even when things get busy.

## What’s been your favourite place to play so far?

[Thuishaven](https://thuishaven.nl/) is a favourite. I really love playing for Dutch crowds, and that’s a place I’m always happy to come back to.

## Where can we hear your music?

Mostly on [SoundCloud](https://soundcloud.com/davyboii), where you can find my tracks and mixes. My releases are also on Spotify, Apple Music and the other usual platforms.

## What one song would feature on the soundtrack to your life?

“Tokyo Drift” by Teriyaki Boyz. I trained as a car mechanic and got into tuning cars quite early. That song reminds me of that time, which I look back on really fondly. It always puts me in a good mood.

## What motivates you?

Knowing that people have made an effort to come and see me. Some bring their friends, some travel quite far, and some have been looking forward to that night for a while. I really appreciate that. Seeing them enjoy themselves makes me want to keep improving and give them a reason to come back.

## Tell us an interesting fact about yourself.

I get up and dance to my tracks after working on them. It helps me hear things differently. Sometimes a section seems fine while I’m sitting at the laptop, but when I’m moving to it, I realise it goes on too long. So dancing around my room is actually part of the process.

## Complete this sentence: At heart I’m just a…

…raver who ended up behind the decks.

## What’s the best bit of advice you’ve received?

“Your problems are someone else’s dreams.” I take it as a reminder to appreciate what I get to do. It helps me keep some perspective.

## Where will you be in five years’ time?

I’d love to reach more people with my music and make something that means something to them, whether it helps them through a difficult day or becomes a song they share with their friends. Knowing that something I made could become a small part of someone’s life would mean a lot to me.

**Davyboi and DJ Cringey "Naughty" is out now. [Listen on Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/track/67MB3IlBzSxG6Q9SGh7qXF?si=3fcc2aea3dfb4851). Buy on Bandcamp.**

**Find Davyboi on [Instagram.](https://www.instagram.com/iamdavyboi/?hl=en)**

**Don’t have Ableton Live? Buy it [↗ ableton.com](https://www.ableton.com/shop/live/?affiliate=F4nlA735). Heads up, it’s an affiliate link. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission (it doesn’t affect the price).**

items.articleBody:
When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled *Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories*. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

## Fostering connections and reflection

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. [Uri Hasson](https://blog.ted.com/what-happens-in-the-brain-when-we-hear-stories-uri-hasson-at-ted2016/) and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”

Even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at [UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft/oral-history-center) for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:

> I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

## Providing unique perspectives

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

According to the [Oral History Association](https://oralhistory.org/), “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of [Voice of Witness](https://voiceofwitness.org/), a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate issues and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

While oral histories are limited to an individuals’ memories and are by nature subjective, they remain incredibly valuable in their ability to paint a portrait of time and place. Plus, their narrative-driven format brings history to life in a more memorable way than date- and fact-focused textbooks.

Helen Marks, a former history teacher who has spoken to thousands of students about her experience as a hidden child in Belgium during World War II, has observed that when a person shares their stories, it brings that part of history to life:

> I am among the few surviving hidden children who are willing and able to talk about their experiences in the Holocaust. Reading numbers on a page does not create the same impact as someone standing or sitting in front of you describing a moment that was frightening or was so foreign they didn’t know what to do.... I think that when you connect a face, no matter what the face looks like, you get a wholly different reaction than when you read a page full of facts.

## Leaving a legacy

Throughout the interviews I conducted for *Folk Life*, the importance of leaving a meaningful legacy was a common theme. “That’s the reason we share our stories,” says Marsha Higgins, a history teacher for nearly 40 years. “It makes us feel like we matter.”

Higgins taught students to create personal narratives from a young age. Decades later, former students still express their thanks for her guidance in teaching them the importance of recording their experiences.

“I encouraged students to write down things that happened to them. It’s helpful to know at the time, you’re creating chapters in your life, that your story is just as interesting as anybody else’s.”

Like Marks, Higgins grew up around immigrants from Europe. “And they all had stories,” she says. “Whenever we got together, somebody would tell me a story. How do you make conversation without one? It’s just so much a part of who we are.”

“I think everyone wants to know that they have made a positive difference,” says Marks. “That they did some good, that their being here wasn’t just a fleeting moment of nothingness, but that they contributed something. They reacted to something. They gave something. So when you tell stories, that’s where you learn about people and what they value.”

## Gaining newfound awareness

Neal Allen, a coach and author (most recently of *Good Writing: 36 Ways to Improve Your Sentences* with his wife Anne Lamott), spent several years as a hospice volunteer. During that time, he helped a number of people share and record their stories.

“Every week I had one or two clients who were dying, and I spent time fluffing their pillows, listening to their stories and how they approach death. The funny thing is we were always asked, ‘Oh, isn’t that hard?’ It was quite the opposite. It was really quite extraordinary.”

A seasoned journalist, Allen knew how to ask evocative questions. “Oddball memories were coming up that hadn’t come up in 50 years maybe,” he says, which led to more and more stories. “My subjects would get really involved in it. To finish their story, it would take eight to 12 hours, sometimes up to 40 hours.”

Allen wrote a biography about his father, which proved to be a learning opportunity for both him and his brothers:

> Once [the book] was bound and we read it all the way through, we had the same reaction, ‘Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, did you know about that?’ Our second reaction was, ‘We’re not in it,’ and burst out laughing. It was easy to laugh about because he never, ever gave us any sign that he disapproved of us in any fundamental way.

For older adults, sharing stories not only connects them with family, each other, and audiences, it also exercises the brain and fosters a sense of well-being. Story sharing activates memory networks while encouraging reflection on past experiences.

[Reminiscence therapy](https://www.nature.com/nature-index/topics/l4/reminiscence-therapy-for-enhancing-mental-health-in-older-adults), a structured method of helping individuals recall, organize, and share life stories, has proven helpful in elevating people’s moods, enhancing their self-esteem, resolving conflict, and promoting meaning. This mode of therapy is becoming increasingly popular as a way to support seniors facing cognitive decline as well as mental health challenges.

## Storytelling brings us together

Ehrlich notes that more than ever, hearing or reading about others’ stories is a powerful tool for building bridges, especially in this divisive climate.

“We have so much more in common than not,” she says, noting that “there’s a desperate need to understand each other better. Oral history is perhaps a tool for seeing beyond our rigid ideas of who people are and breaking through into a fuller understanding.”

“What always astonished the subject of the memoirs was how many people they had touched,” says Allen. “I think we touch a far greater number of people than we can hold or remember at any one time.”

In this way, sharing stories reminds us that our interactions have more of an impact than we realize, not only in our close-knit circles, but also at work, at school, and even in everyday exchanges.

What sharing our stories boils down to, Ehrlich believes, is that it’s a fundamental human instinct:

> How do we live a life? How do we deal with joy and difficulty and disappointment and pleasure? How do we make choices? What do we have control over? What don’t we have control over? Oral histories, at their most basic, include all the stuff that makes us people, including our desire to be seen, heard, and understood. And everybody’s stories matter.

items.subtitle: Die Open-Source Community hat Rolands Plug-Out Technologie geknackt und ermöglicht mit einem neuen Software Development Kit die Entwicklung eigener…
items.feedText:
Welche alternativen Plug-Outs gibt es mittlerweile? Und Roland …? Links

Open-Source Plug-Outs für System-1 und System-8

items.articleBody:
**Die Open-Source Community hat Rolands Plug-Out Technologie geknackt und ermöglicht mit einem neuen Software Development Kit die Entwicklung eigener Synthesizer für [System-1](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/roland-aira-system-1-test/) und System-8.**

System-1 und System-8 (Bildquelle: Roland)

Inhalte

- Open-Source Plug-Outs für System-1 und System-8
- Das Plug-Out SDK für System 1 und System 8
- Wo finde ich das Open Source Projekt?
- Welche alternativen Plug-Outs gibt es mittlerweile?
- Und Roland …?
- Links

## Open-Source Plug-Outs für System-1 und System-8

Nun erleben wir einen weiteren Höhepunkt der Open Source Bewegung: Wie allgemein bekannt sein dürfte, handelt es sich beim [Roland System-1](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/roland-aira-system-1-test/) und System-8 nicht nur um Hardware Synthesizer. Beide Instrumente sind mit Rolands Plugout Technologie ausgestattet, die es ermöglicht, zusätzliche Synthesizer aus der Roland Cloud auf die Hardware zu laden. Für den System 1 gibt es z.B. den SH-101, SH-2, Primars und das System-100. Es handelt sich um ein geschlossenes System, denn nur Roland Plug-Outs sind erlaubt. Doch das hat sich jetzt geändert.

Es ist übrigens nicht das erste Mal, dass sich die Community einen Roland Synthesizer zur Brust nimmt. Erst vor wenigen Wochen beziehungsweise Monaten sind alternative Betriebssysteme für den Roland SP 404 MK2 aufgetaucht.

## Das Plug-Out SDK für System 1 und System 8

Enorrmann hat trotz der Beschränkungen von Roland die Plug-Out Technologie durch Reverse Engineering entschlüsselt. Sein Ziel war es nicht nur, Plug-Outs für die beiden Roland Sysnsthsizer zu entwickeln, sondern ein Software Development Kit (SDK) bereitzustellen.

Dies erlaubt es jedem, Plug-Outs für System-1 und System-8 zu entwickeln. Offensichtlich ist es auch möglich, die Limitierungen der Hardware aufzuheben. Wie allgemein bekannt, war das System 1 ursprünglich auf vier Stimmen beschränkt. Jetzt gibt es schon Plug-Outs mit 6 oder 8 Stimmen.

## Wo finde ich das Open Source Projekt?

Hier geht es zum[Roland-Plugout-Reveng Website auf GitHub](https://github.com/enorrmann/roland-plugout-reveng) von Enorrmann.

System-1 (Bildquelle: Roland)

## Welche alternativen Plug-Outs gibt es mittlerweile?

Inzwischen wurden mehrere Synthesizer mithilfe seines SDK entwickelt. Dazu gehören ein sechsstimmiger Mutable String Polysynth, zwei Casio CZ artige Polysynthesizer mit sechs beziehungsweise acht Stimmen, ein Poly 6, ein achtstimmiger Synthesizer im Stil des JX 3P, der Supersaw Poly7 sowie ein Synthesizer im Stil der TB 03.

## Und Roland …?

Wie Roland auf diese Entwicklung reagieren wird, ist derzeit völlig offen. Ob der Hersteller die Aktivitäten der Community unterstützt, duldet oder möglicherweise dagegen vorgeht, steht in den Sternen. Fest steht jedoch, dass es ausgesprochen interessant ist, auf welche Weise sich die Open Source Community Rolands Hardware zu eigen macht und welche neuen Möglichkeiten sich daraus ergeben.

System-1 (Bildquelle: Roland)

items.articleBody:
Einmal mehr warnt der Signal Messenger vor dem Zugriff von KI-Assistenten auf eigentlich private und verschlüsselte Kommunikation. Der Messenger führt deswegen neue Sicherheitsmaßnahmen ein. Das Problem ist aber grundsätzlicher.

Wenn KI-Assistenten Chats mitlesen, kann niemand mehr für die Privatsphäre dieser Chats garantieren. (Symbolbild) – Gemeinfrei-ähnlich freigegeben durch unsplash.com: [Claudio Schwarz](https://unsplash.com/de/fotos/ein-weisser-kuhlschrank-mit-einem-schwarzen-aufkleber-auf-dem-steht-wer-zuschaut-9XFwNI21Qsk)

Es ist ein Verdienst von Messenger-Apps wie Signal, Threema und sogar WhatsApp, dass heute so viel private Kommunikation wie noch nie verschlüsselt ist. Durch den Einbau sicherer Verschlüsselung für alle haben sie maßgeblich zum Schutz der Privatsphäre von Milliarden Menschen beigetragen. Doch dieser Erfolg ist gerade massiv in Gefahr. Durch den galoppierenden Einzug von praktischen KI-Assistenten droht die technisch aufwendig verschlüsselte Kommunikation aus den Apps herauszufließen, um an Googles Gemini oder Apples Siri AI verfüttert zu werden.

Die schön verschlüsselte Familienchatgruppe ist nämlich nicht mehr privat, wenn Onkel Dieter seinen KI-Assistenten darüber laufen lässt, damit dieser ihm die Inhalte zusammenfasst. Das gilt auch für politische Chatgruppen oder die von Unternehmen und Behörden. Immer dann, wenn jemand die KI mit den Chat-Inhalten füttert, führt er letztlich die mühsam errungene IT-Sicherheit ad absurdum und liefert alle anderen Chatmitglieder dem Zugriff von Dritten auf die Kommunikation aus. Da hilft auch die beste Verschlüsselung nicht mehr.

## Signal führt Sicherheitsvorkehrungen ein

Schon beim vergangenen Chaos Communication Congress [hatten Vertreter:innen von Signal in einem Vortrag (Video)](https://media.ccc.de/v/39c3-ai-agent-ai-spy) vor dieser Bedrohung der Kommunikation gewarnt, nun ergreift der Messenger Maßnahmen. Laut einer [Mitteilung im Blog](https://signal.org/blog/protecting-your-privacy/) führt Signal in der kommenden Version neue Sicherheitsvorkehrungen ein, die verhindern sollen, dass KI-Assistenten, die in die mobilen Betriebssysteme Android und iOS integriert sind, auf vertrauliche Nachrichten der Nutzer:innen zugreifen oder diese erfassen.

Schon im letzten Jahr hatte Signal bei der Desktop-Version auf Windows-Rechnern [der KI-Funktion „Recall“ von Microsofts KI Copilot verboten](https://signal.org/blog/signal-doesnt-recall/), standardmäßig Screenshots von Signal-Nachrichten aufzunehmen und zu speichern.

Hintergrund der neuen Maßnahmen ist nun, dass Apple und Google KI-Assistenten in ihre Betriebssysteme integrieren und die Programme, die auf den Bildschirmen angezeigten Informationen erfassen können. Dabei können vertrauliche Informationen an KI-Dienste weitergegeben werden, die außerhalb der Kontrolle der jeweiligen App liegen.

Um das Risiko für die Privatsphäre zu mindern, schränkt Signal dafür die Erstellung von Screenshots seiner App unter iOS 27 und Android ein – und zwar immer dann, wenn erkannt wird, dass ein KI-Assistent versucht, auf den Bildschirminhalt zuzugreifen, heißt es in der deutschen Pressemitteilung. Dabei sei der Schutz standardmäßig aktiviert. Nutzer:innen können allerdings diesen Schutz in den Einstellungen von Signal deaktivieren – sie machen dadurch aber die Kommunikation für sich und ihre Gesprächspartner:innen unsicherer.

Last week, [Apple announced](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/11/meet-the-2026-app-store-award-finalists/) the finalists for the 2026 App Store Awards. The App Store Awards are Apple’s annual celebration of exceptional apps and games across 12 categories spanning the company’s platforms. It’s an excellent collection that includes solo developers, small indie teams, big companies, and many MacStories favorites.

Here’s the complete list of finalists:

### iPhone App of the Year

### iPhone Game of the Year

### iPad App of the Year

### iPad Game of the Year

### Mac App of the Year

### Mac Game of the Year

### Apple Arcade Game of the Year

### Apple Vision Pro App of the Year

### Apple Vision Pro Game of the Year

### Apple Watch App of the Year

### Apple TV App of the Year

### Cultural Impact Apps

### Cultural Impact Games

This year’s App Store Awards finalists showcase just how much depth and breadth there is on the App Store. Apple has come up with an excellent list of finalists, which includes many MacStories favorites, like Paste, (Not Boring) Camera, Things, Ulysses, Pocket Casts, Big Walk, BALL x PIT, and many others you should check out.

Soon, we’ll hear who won each category, but I appreciate that Apple publishes the list of finalists because any of these apps would be a great pick as the winner of its category. Congratulations to all the finalists. It’s quite an honor to be recognized as one of the best among the millions of apps and games on the App Store, and it’s great to see the hard work that went into each of these apps recognized.

items.articleBody:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

## Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\ \left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ {\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\ \left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ \left(t\right) \times \ {|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \ \left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\ \left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\ \left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\ \left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\ \left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\ a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\ $$

Where:

$$
\ {lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\ (0) \times \ (1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\ $$

This captures a few things:

- The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.
- The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.
- The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\ $. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, because these represent situations where the tangents have been flipped by 180º.

In most cases, there will only be one valid solution, and this works pretty well:

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

## Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, it's about to vanish, so its weight should go to zero there.

2) When two opposite-bending parabolas are about to become tangent, two solutions will move towards each other, before both vanishing at the same time:

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\ = \ 2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\ \\[0.3em]
\ = \ b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\ $$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \ \cdot \ }{\displaystyle |\ ||\ |}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\ |$ i.e. $\ $, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \left(\ {\displaystyle |\ |^2}\right)^2
$$

- By applying $\arccos \left(-\cos \theta\right)$, we remap the dot-product range $(-1..1)$ to $(0..π)$ which effectively neutralizes the unstable solutions
- Large $|\ |$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option
- When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \ {|\ - \ |^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

## Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

*The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/unconed/bezbox/-/blob/master/src/graph/bez.ts?ref_type=heads#L61).*

items.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
items.subtitle:
Hayward, Guy Sella

When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response?
items.feedText: Hayward, Guy Sella When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed.
items.articleBody: When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

What you will learn about:

How 3GPP standards from Release 15 to Release 19 built the foundation of NR-NTN, and why NTN extends 5G coverage to oceans, rural regions, and disaster zones.

How transparent and regenerative satellite payload architectures differ, and what each choice means for round trip time, link budget, and hardware complexity.

Why long distances, fast-moving satellites, and Doppler shift challenge the physical layer, including synchronization, timing advance, and HARQ operation.

How mobility works in NTN, including cell selection, conditional handover, feeder link switchover, and movement between terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks.

How to test NTN devices, satellites, and networks with RF, protocol, and over-the-air methods under realistic fading and propagation conditions.

How NTN evolves toward 6G unified networks that combine multiple bands, layers, and dimensions, with sensing, positioning, and AI.

Download this free whitepaper now!

## The Debt Trap (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/23/grasshoppers-v-ants/#)

Smoking is very stupid. I was a smoker for 17 years, from ages 13-30. I was very stupid to start smoking. That stupidity only came into sharper focus a few years ago, when I got a cancer diagnosis (don't worry, I am now cancer-free):

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail](https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail)

In my defense, I'll point out that I was just a kid when I started, but also, smoking belongs to a class of pernicious problems whose insidiousness is rooted in the distance between their causes and effects:

[https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/](https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/)

I've often said that if a little tumor had sprouted immediately after I took my first puff, I never would have taken a second one. Now that I've actually had the experience of being told that I have a tumor, I can say *definitively* that I would not have taken that second puff. An economist would tell you that I was engaged in "hyperbolic discounting": underpricing a future cost and overvaluing a present pleasure:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting)

But I don't think that tells the whole story. Sure, I was engaged in hyperbolic discounting, but *why* was I doing that? What was it about smoking (as opposed to, say, French-kissing light-sockets) that led me to apply a hyperbolic discount to the costs of smoking? I say it was the attenuated relationship between cause and effect. It's not just that we undervalue the price of smoking: it's that we struggle to arrive at a correct price for smoking in the moment, because the intellectual knowledge of cancer statistics is in no way comparable to the visceral experience of a cancer diagnosis. Estimating the "cost" (emotional, physiological, monetary) of a cancer diagnosis is *hard*, especially if you're young and have had the good fortune of a life untouched by close contact with agonizing illness and death.

The point I'm making is that the discount isn't just hyperbolic, it's hyperbolic *because* it relies so much upon guesswork, without comparable experiences to anchor your estimate.

What's more, it's this same *attenuated causality* (in which cause is separated from effect by so much time and space) that allowed the tobacco industry to sow so much profitable doubt about the connection between smoking and cancer. Sure, *some* of the policymakers who let Big Tobacco off the hook were doubtlessly in their pocket, reliant on campaign contributions or beholden to a party that was in some queasy, cozy relationship with these death merchants. But the reason Big Tobacco was able ( *is* able) to get away with killing us for so many decades is that you don't get a tumor with each puff.

I believe that *most* of the policymakers who reasoned their way into doubting the connection between smoking and cancer were ensnared by this attenuated causality. They might have had low morals and low intellect, but the factor that made them such easy marks for Big Tobacco's death-hustlers was this wide, long gap between cause and effect.

This cuts both ways: if you're a policymaker of low intellect and morals, you can rig your policies to put their consequences a long way off in the future, which might give you time to escape to a lucrative private-sector career with the industrial interests who benefited from your chicanery. Or (if you're a Mitch McConnell-adjacent flesh-eating ghoul who plans to die only after centuries in office, chin red and slick with the heartblood of the innocent), you can put so much time and space between your fuckery and the ruin it brings that the voting public fails to connect your actions with the consequences. After all, no one ever lost money betting against the American public's object permanence.

For example, Trump's Big Bill was designed to make its deepest cuts – to Medicaid, rural hospitals, the increased tax-load on workers to advantage their bosses – *after* the midterm elections. The cynical reasoning isn't hard to follow: We'll just tell voters that all the bad things they've been told about the coming cuts are Fake News, and then, after the cuts arrive, blame their post-midterm misery on Biden, communists, trans people, immigrants, and the phases of the moon.

This cheap trick may be deplorable, but you should also save some anger for politicians who enact *good* policies but refuse to take account of this principle. Take Biden's 2021 plan to lower prescription drug prices. This started off as a rule that would end the longstanding, outrageous policy that bans Medicare/Medicaid from negotiating with pharma companies. Yes, you read that right: when Uncle Sucker buys drugs from Big Pharma, the government just asks the pharma companies how much public money they'd like, and then the USA writes the companies a check for whatever sum they name, no questions asked. That's why the US pays 300% more than any other advanced nation for its drugs.

Thus Biden's initial proposal: let Medicare/Medicaid negotiate drug prices the same way every private insurer *and* every public health system does. But then, Biden's team allowed that policy to be diluted so that it would only apply to *ten* drugs, and *only* if those drugs had been on the market for at least 13 years. Finally, *the piece de resistance*: the plan wasn't design to kick in until 2025, *after* the 2024 election, which turned out to be a referendum on the cost of living (including drug prices) that saw the Dems getting their asses kicked by the stupidest, most obviously corrupt fascists in American electoral history:

[https://pluralistic.net/2021/11/18/bipartisan-consensus/#corruption](https://pluralistic.net/2021/11/18/bipartisan-consensus/#corruption)

Whether you're ignoring attenuated causality or weaponizing it, it's critical to any analysis of how we get into as much trouble as we do. It is the ruin of individuals and firms, and of political and economic systems.

Take vaccinations: herd immunity requires a *lot* of compliance: nearly all of us have to get vaccinated before the real benefits kick in. Securing this compliance takes a lot of effort, because the system has to get people to invest their faith in the prospect that *eventually* we'll get to herd immunity and an end to infection.

But once herd immunity is in place, noncompliance is a much smaller deal. The very fact of herd immunity means that people can opt out here or there without getting sick (because *we're* all up-to-date on *our* vaccinations). Worse, the very fact of herd immunity means that after a while, no one can really remember what the sickness was like: we think of measles as something the Little Rascals pretended to have so they could play hooky, not as a terrifyingly infectious disease that can leave you blind or brain damaged. Asking someone who's never lived through a measles epidemic to estimate the cost of measles is like asking a 13 year old to estimate what a cancer diagnosis will feel like.

The same applies to antitrust enforcement. An economy of small and medium sized firms who compete with one another is an economy where workers have more bargaining leverage and regulators don't have to worry about being outspent and outlasted with decade-plus appeals when they crack down on corrupt businesses:

[https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/15/business/us-vsibm.html](https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/15/business/us-vsibm.html)

It's also an economy where companies must compete rather than collude. Look at what happened to the ad-tech industry, which is dominated by a duopoly that controls 80% of display advertising, and that duopoly has an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the market to pay publishers less and charge advertisers more:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue)

In the post-war era, antitrust enforcers did their jobs: they blocked mergers, punished predatory pricing, and aggressively investigated sweetheart deals between retail incumbents and their suppliers that were designed to freeze out new businesses:

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities](https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities)

This produced an economy where companies had lower profits, because workers and consumers could force them to disgorge more of their surpluses, and because they had to invest more in improving their offerings to keep up with competitors. It was an economy where prosperity was more broadly shared and where it was easier to impose democratic accountability on the private sector.

Then, starting with Jimmy Carter, America turned its back on antitrust. Year after year, presidency after presidency, enforcers waved through larger and more anticompetitive mergers and ignored more egregious predatory practices. For 50 years, the neoclassical economists who promoted this *laissez-faire* doctrine have smugly pointed out that even though the economy grew more consolidated thanks to their policy, we still *had* an economy, one that was often booming, where politicians could (sometimes) be seen to be intervening to address corporate cheating.

The public, meanwhile, has historically struggled to connect the problems of oligarchy with these pro-oligarch policies. They can feel the regulatory capture, they know that labor grows weaker every year, they are furious at their sellout politicians and the system's naked corruption. But because the policy is separated from its outcomes by so much time and space, there's lots of room for the policy's architects and beneficiaries to do the economic version of denying the link between smoking and cancer; that is, denying the link between pro-monopoly policies and monopolies.

Attenuated causality lets bad-faith actors sell us anti-vax, pro-monopoly, cancer denial…and, of course, climate denial. NASA's James Hansen warned Congress about climate change in 1988. It's not like the oil companies didn't know about this. As far back as the 1970s, Exxon's own scientists had warned the company about global warming, and the company took actions based on those warnings:

[https://insideclimatenews.org/project/exxon-the-road-not-taken/](https://insideclimatenews.org/project/exxon-the-road-not-taken/)

Mobil, meanwhile, started secretly raising its drilling platforms to account for rising seas, even as it was taking out full-page ads in national daily newspapers that stated that "The science of climate change is too uncertain to mandate a plan of action":

[https://web.archive.org/web/20160101024248/http://graphics.latimes.com/oil-operations/](https://web.archive.org/web/20160101024248/http://graphics.latimes.com/oil-operations/)

Attenuated causality was and is at the core of climate denial. If every climate-shredding gas turbine that the self-described environmental hero Elon Musk fired up at one of his AI data-centers immediately caused a flood or a wildfire or a heat-wave, we'd scrape all those data-centers down to their foundation slabs and then we'd display Musk in stocks and pelt him with rotten fruit.

Musk really knows how to turn attenuated causality to his advantage. Remember when he performatively borrowed a security guard's pocket knife and started slicing through the Ethernet cables connecting Twitter's servers?

[https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2023-09-14/when-elon-musk-unplugged-the-twitter-servers-with-a-pocket-knife-theres-still-shit-thats-broken-because-of-it.html](https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2023-09-14/when-elon-musk-unplugged-the-twitter-servers-with-a-pocket-knife-theres-still-shit-thats-broken-because-of-it.html)

Or when he started shutting down whole data-centers and mass-firing Twitter's technical staff?

[https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/29/technology/twitter-elon-musk.html](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/29/technology/twitter-elon-musk.html)

The point of this performance was to let Musk claim that Twitter's management had let itself be gulled by featherbedding engineers who grossly overbuilt Twitter's infrastructure in order to guarantee themselves perpetual employment at the expense of Twitter's shareholders. But all that spare server capacity wasn't excess: it was the cushion, the headroom, the insurance policy. Those were the servers that would pick up the slack when another server lost its power-supply or caught a bad stick of RAM. They were the servers that could shoulder the load during the next 9/11 or Arab Spring. They were the engineering staff that could execute new projects or perform emergency maintenance – and the engineering staff that could plan the next build-out in advance so that future growth wouldn't stall out when Twitter ran out of hardware.

Musk's actions didn't occur in a vacuum. During the decades in which attenuated causality set the scene for an endless, incestuous orgy of mergers and acquisitions, it became normal for business leaders to hack away at their own firms' resiliency. University administrators fired tenured professors and replaced them with casualized, proletarianized adjuncts.

The pedagogy – and the universities' reputations – persisted after the cuts, ebbing away slowly as the institutional memory and standards eroded bit by bit. But eventually, the universities found themselves in crisis. Campuses erupted in student revolt and spectacular scenes of violent repression:

[https://jayrosen.tumblr.com/post/13174138991/excerpt-from-uc-davis-2010-2012-general-catalog](https://jayrosen.tumblr.com/post/13174138991/excerpt-from-uc-davis-2010-2012-general-catalog)

Universities' reputations cratered and they found themselves easy pickings for demagogues who awarded themselves a veto over faculty, curriculum and admissions:

[https://www.chronicle.com/article/columbia-capitulated-but-so-did-the-rest-of-higher-ed](https://www.chronicle.com/article/columbia-capitulated-but-so-did-the-rest-of-higher-ed)

That's the thing about attenuated causality: it lets people and institutions and systems play a high-stakes game of Jenga in which every non-load-bearing block is removed and added to the top of the teetering stack. No one block causes the system to collapse…until one block does, and the whole thing falls over.

It's like an avalanche. Drop one snowflake after another on the mountainside. Expose it to the midday sun and the frigid night. Sure, it creaks. Watch closely and you'll see it make minute shifts. Every now and again, a light scree of snow slides off the surface and skitters downhill, but the great mass of snow is stable.

Until it isn't. Until one last snowflake alights on the mountainside and sets the whole thing rumbling and tumbling in an inexorable, unstoppable wall of snow that only halts when it can go no lower.

The run-up to an avalanche is a long, long series of linear phenomena. A snowflake is minute. Add it to the pile and it will produce a minute effect. A little bit of heat causes a little bit of expansion. A little bit of wind blows a little of the loose cover around. But each one of these little strains on the system makes it less stable overall. The snowpack's stability is invisible. A snowpack that is about to cut loose is indistinguishable from one that will stay put for weeks or months. But once the snow's systemic resiliency has been exhausted, the next linear perturbation produces a wild, catastrophic, nonlinear collapse.

Attenuated causality lets us build up a mountain of debt: health debt, technology debt, policy debt, credibility debt. It's impossible to know when the system's homeostatic mechanisms have been fatally weakened, such that the next compromise it is asked to bear causes it to rupture, or implode, or crumble.

We can raise the level of CO2 and methane in the Earth's atmosphere year after year and see long-attenuated, linear effects: fires here, floods there, some extinctions. But one day: we overwhelm some invisible homeostatic mechanism and we lose the Gulf Stream:

[https://www.bbc.com/climate/impact/gulf_stream.shtml](https://www.bbc.com/climate/impact/gulf_stream.shtml)

Same goes for the world's IT: we can fire IT workers, starve maintenance teams of budget and personnel, substitute indemnity for software quality, allow our "security" agencies to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities, and on average, it will all work…until it stops:

[https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake](https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake)

IT might just be the most dangerously attenuated aspect of all our administrative functions. A software engineer writes a piece of code and it keeps running, even if you fire that engineer. This is one of the reasons it's so hard to unionize tech workers: when they go on strike, their scab software crosses the picket line and keeps working:

[https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook)

But software isn't an asset, it's a liability. Code runs in a *system*, with upstream processes that produce its inputs and downstream processes that operate on its outputs. There's adjacent processes, too: other software that also gets fed by those upstream processes and also feeds those downstream processes. Even if the code never changes, the system the code is part of changes constantly, which means that the more code you have, the more code you have to maintain.

So what happens when you fire technical workers is nothing…at first. And then, bit by bit, things start to break. And break. And break. Only the people who wrote the software – and the people they trained through working alongside of them – know exactly how it works, with that deep knowledge, that *Fingerspitzengefühl*, that informs their intuition so they can figure out why things broke and how to fix them:

[https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/08/process-knowledge/#dance-monkey-dance](https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/08/process-knowledge/#dance-monkey-dance)

Break that chain of knowledge and you lobotomize your institution. Reduce the full complement of experienced engineers with the wherewithal to demand higher wages and better conditions, leave behind a precarious skeleton crew of juniors you terrorize with layoff threats and AI ghost-stories, and you destroy not just your ability to spot problems before they occur, but also your capability to salvage your way out of the wreckage.

And that's what Musk's Doge did to the American state: undermined its capacity to absorb shocks, to anticipate shocks and brace for them – or even to detect the shocks when they're underway. There's a reason so much variation is preserved in our genomes and species: these are the reserves of variety that can rise to meet the changing world. Eliminate the variety, and you strip out the ability to cope with surprise, and what happens next shouldn't surprise any of us.
