items.articleBody:
[Janet Flanner-Solita Solano papers](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/95507085/), Library of Congress. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Georges_Gurdjieff.JPG).

My first mistake was to draw a connection. The flyers appeared all at once over the telephone poles of my neighborhood in the East Bay, with contact info provided on the kind of tear-away strips more typical of a HELP WANTED or FOR SALE notice, only here the subject read: AN INTRODUCTORY DISCUSSION: G. I. GURDJIEFF. The accompanying copy spoke of spiritual methods and cosmic scale; the words seemed to promise some tremendous synthesis between part and whole, spirit and matter, individual and collective. More prosaically, they advertised a series of public meetings to take place in Berkeley. My second mistake, I think, was to write an email expressing interest.

Where had I heard the name Gurdjieff? The question took me several minutes of standing in front of the poster to answer. I must have missed the crossing signal before remembering with a start that the life’s work of the Russian-born mystic, teacher, sacred choreographer, and occasional composer of piano music [George Ivanovich Gurdjieff](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2020/10/22/the-lesbian-partnership-that-changed-literature/) had—for me at least—everything to do with a small, neglected corner in the [short fiction](https://www.theparisreview.org/authors/4476/joy-williams) of [Joy Williams](https://www.theparisreview.org/authors/4476/joy-williams).

Photograph by Drew Dickerson.

“Gurdjieff in the Sunshine State” appears in Williams’s 1990 book *Escapes,* but is among the very few stories not to make it into her nearly comprehensive collection *The Visiting Privilege*, published twenty-five years later. I have never understood the logic behind its exclusion any more than I can claim to understand the story itself—in which G. astral projects to Florida, where, as a specter, he observes a roller rink, drinks a Tab, and chats briefly with what may be the ghost of Katherine Mansfield. By virtue of being disincluded from Williams’s collected work, this story of an esotericist feels in turn to have become itself esoteric, tucked away and little read. Even Williams’s own mentions of the story seemed charged with the force of mystery. “There is a Gurdjieff story in Escapes,” she wrote to her editor, the late Gary Fisketjon, in 2011. “I was going to write a whole mess of these stories on Gurdjieff but haven’t, you’re probably happy to know.”

The historical Gurdjieff was no stranger to hermetic situations. He traveled widely during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In the course of his itinerary between the Mediterranean and southwest Asia, he absorbed the teachings that would result in his syncretistic blend of Sufi, Hindu, Zen, and Christian tendencies. But the articulation of his thought in a system and set of practices later known as the Fourth Way would come to be passed between generations, making Gurdjieff one of the most influential figures in what we today call the New Age Movement.

Some of this biographical picture was imparted at the first public meeting I attended in the auxiliary room of a Unitarian Universalists Fellowship Hall. For practical purposes the scene might have been lifted straight out of the fiction of Williams herself—from “The Country,” say, in which a group of denominationally wide-ranging seekers meet weekly “in one of the many, many rooms” of an Episcopal church to discuss the question: “Why Are We Here?”

I took my seat in a circle of folding chairs under a framed black-and-white portrait of Gurdjieff that someone had arrived early to hang. It was the first time I’d seen a picture of him. His eyes were enormous. Introductory talk proceeded gnomically. Most present seemed to have been steeped in one or another Gurdjieff-adjacent current. All were capable of trading words as tokens in a kind of code I had trouble grasping.

“I was brought here out of interest in the work of Maurice Nicoll.”

“Yes, well. Nicoll certainly had a lot to say, didn’t he? Maybe he ran out of things to say by the time of his fifth book. You should read Ouspensky.”

“I’m wary of Ouspensky. Remember what Gurdjieff told him: if you understood half of what you know, you’d be my teacher.”

Why were we there? Newcomers were encouraged to share our answers to this question. I owned up to my literary detective work in tracking down this reference of Williams’s, so marginal in her body of work as to be secretive. I also said that I wanted to enjoy a closer relationship to [God](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2013/06/03/3-stories-of-god/), which was true.

Motivations varied. One woman mentioned a near-death experience several months ago that convinced her of the need for greater spiritual attunement. Another spoke about how, after a childhood spent being told to shut up, she was now emboldened to want to find her voice. Someone else detailed a fairly fresh LSD episode before producing a decorative knife that he told us had been forged from the metal of an authentic meteorite. The ceremonial blade looked no shorter than six inches.

Georges Gurdjieff, 1930. [Time](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Time_-_1930.03.24_-_62_-_Georges_Gurdjieff.png), Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Time_-_1930.03.24_-_62_-_Georges_Gurdjieff.png).

*Experience* certainly struck me as a keyword in the group’s talk, in the sense of a spiritual experience’s spontaneous flash of insight that leaves one wholly changed. *Vibration*, too, was in frequent currency. *Self-observation*. *Self-knowledge. Self-remembering.* One first-time visitor’s chancing upon the term *wish* was met with a gasp. The wish, it seemed, was fundamental. The lights were dimmed. The scent of patchouli was strong. Boredom was my prevailing attitude—shot through at odd intervals with the numinous feeling that somehow anything at all might be possible.

Others seemed less impressed. An attendee identifying himself as a veteran of workshops in human development at the Esalen Institute complained, not without cause, that we’d certainly heard the name Gurdjieff plenty. But what did he teach in specific terms? What did he promise? We’d been told Gurdjieff had answers. I felt my own small disappointment with the session, mired in personal anecdote, without much in the way of a survey of Gurdjieff’s system.

“You’re right to ask,” said one man. “Gurdjieff works by allegory. He says of his writing in *All and Everything*: ‘I bury the bone so deep that the dogs have to scratch for it.’”

The second of Williams’s Gurdjieff stories is titled “George and Susan”; it was published in a 2014 issue of *Tin House* before appearing in her most recent collection, *The Pelican Child*. Again Gurdjieff appears on the page initialized as G.—a nod, perhaps, to P. D. Ouspensky’s memoir *In Search of the Miraculous*, which refers to the teacher only by this initial. In Williams’s story, G. haunts the childhood residence of Susan Sontag in Tucson, where Williams herself lives, and seems possibly to witness a car crash.

Something in Gurdjieff’s travels across state lines at last felt to me to possess the principle of a series. As if sense might be made through dint of sheer repetition. As though there might be a Gurdjieff story for every state in the Union. Why is it that fifty seems more plausible than two? “It is only through effort,” reads one aside in “George and Susan,” “through will, through work work work that two becomes extraordinary.”

This contemplative dimension has always been what I’ve responded to most in Williams’s stories—concerned as they are with their own buried dog bones and esoteric disclosures. Williams’s fiction is full to the brim with prophetic significance, the veiling and unveiling of messages, quasi-theological disputation, revelation of the extraordinary within the everyday, the aleatory coincidence of higher and lower worlds. “The short story,” Williams said on a 1991 episode of KCRW’s *Bookworm,* “is the closest thing we have to a moral form. It’s a method in which to really dwell upon—reflect upon—the things that matter.”

Perhaps it was Gurdjieff’s own project of dwelling on “the things that matter” that drew Williams to him as a figure in the first place—his belief that these things, forgotten through dint of daily habit, might be again brought to the surface by force of pain or effort.

I think it must have been in the group’s second public meeting that the terms *shock* and *work* appeared. *Shock* meant not as in an emotion, but instead in the shock of experience, necessary to jolt a person from her unawakened life toward the end of finally, hopefully attaining consciousness of herself. Gurdjieff is said at times to have occasioned such shocks by putting his followers in situations of extraordinary discomfort—demanding that they follow impossibly contradictory instructions, dig ditches to the point of exhaustion, and withstand the rageful tirades into which he seemed capable of entering at random.

“I have a proposal,” said one prominent group member who’d introduced himself as an electrical engineer. “A task. Every morning for the next week, I think we should check in with ourselves and exercise gratitude for this moment as well as the day ahead. Would anyone like to take me up on this?”

“I’ll do it.”

“Me too.”

“I can’t wait to.”

Afterward someone approached me to say they’d read “George and Susan” and found it a trip.

Meanwhile, my own investigations seemed to have stalled. For some weeks I’d shown up, listened patiently, been honest in my intentions—and all I had to show for my efforts was a list of personal and textual coincidences I found hard to draw meaning from. In my life as a graduate student, two separate faculty mentors for two different reasons directed me toward the same sentence in Edward Said’s *On* *Late Style*.

Following up on the indication, I learned that Said’s reference was to Williams’s piece “Hawk,” a personal essay in which she describes sitting down to long hours of piano music during a period of mysterious illness. I was surprised, though I shouldn’t have been, to read her report: “I listened to Thomas de Hartmann play the music of Gurdjieff.” (This hasn’t changed; Williams affirmed as much in an interview with this [magazine](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2025/07/28/ten-questions-for-joy-williams/) last year, referring to de Hartmann and Gurdjieff as “her old friends.”)

I felt compelled to take extraordinary recourse, i.e., violating literary studies’ chief methodological taboo, to never ask an author what she means. I also had a picture postcard featuring a photograph of [Jane Bowles](https://www.theparisreview.org/fiction/3995/emmy-moores-journal-jane-bowles) that I wanted to send to Williams, whose short fiction is everywhere studded with postcards. “In this world there is a postcard of everything,” says a character in “Train,” a favorite of mine. “That’s the kind of world this is.” How does one select just the right picture for a world in which there’s a postcard of everything? Do we aim to please the recipient? Ourselves? I hoped that my selection of Bowles looking assertive in her unkempt mop top might achieve both.

But I was uncertain how to ask after the guru Gurdjieff as an enigmatic minor figure in Williams’s corpus—whether in fact there existed a mystical unpublished center around which the two extant stories might be said to orbit. Postcards are, after all, a tricky medium, sent through the mail without an envelope, the handwritten message plain for any postal worker to see. To pose such a question in the plain light of day felt like a gross indelicacy. (“Whence the postcard,” Jacques Derrida writes in *The Post Card*, “half-private, half-public, neither the one nor the other.”)

My own postcard made it into the mail, at least. Shortly after this I quietly resolved to stop attending the Gurdjieff group. I just couldn’t shake the sense that Gurdjieff’s unique speculative insights had either been intentionally withheld or simply didn’t exist. Which was the worse possibility? It seemed in either case that any answers I sought would remain unforthcoming. Citing a scheduling conflict, I emailed my excuses. In order to awaken, I’d been told, it was first necessary to recognize how one lives in a state of sleep. Maybe I was lacking in mettle to withstand the shock of such an arousal.

On the evening of my first missed meeting I awoke with a start to find myself already on the floor by my bedside. The sensation was like jolting from a dream of falling—except that I had in fact fallen. My flinch of automatic reaction came too late and registered instead as a painful, whole-body wince. I made an ugly noise. I thought I’d been concussed. When I put my fingers to my forehead in the dark they came away sticky. A look in the mirror revealed that my partner and I would have to make an early-morning visit to the emergency room.

I was admitted by a pair of drunk attendants and led to a room where I overheard the sounds of another patient’s shoulder being reset over his screams. I answered the nurse’s questions about my injury, stared into his penlight, followed his gloved finger with my eyes. Yes, I’d fallen out of bed—my forehead seemed to have found the vents of my air purifier on the way down, preventing the impact of a more serious drop. The doctor arrived and applied a glue solution he described to me as having an elegant pine scent. Before I knew it I was patched and discharged, awake before the sun, newly billed a $250 copay, sporting over my left eye a fresh wound that I’d been told was little cause for concern so long as I kept it clean.

That very next morning I checked my inbox to find the following from the group member I’d messaged at the outset of my misadventure:

> You were missed. Thank you for your email. It is much appreciated. Come next week. The meetings continue. I am in Texas this weekend for a movements intensive. I am very interested in how you are responding to the introductory meetings. Perhaps you tried Robert’s task of taking a moment when your feet hit the floor sitting at the edge of your bed being grateful for life and the day ahead.

In the meantime I became comfortable referring to the resulting mark as my Gurdjieff scar. Or else my Joy Williams scar. I was capable of joking that the spirit of Gurdjieff had given me a bump in the night—and sometimes I even believed it. Mostly I kept quiet, embarrassed that an injury should require so much explanation. Now and then it has occurred to me to wonder whether I have been somehow changed or else humbled, made to recognize the vast stretch of the world beyond the extent of the bounds I’d previously thought known. At minimum, my mailbox was not yet done with me, because that’s when I received my postcard response, on its front a midcentury illustration of poolside vacationers to Palm Springs:

> Thanks for the JB card. I don’t have one! Yes, I wanted to do a G collection but my editor at the time, the infamous Gary Fisketjon thought it was nuts. Still—I think—G at the mule dressage events; G at Walden Pond … You should read MAURICE NICOLL and of course OUSPENSKY. Nice hearing from you,
> Joy

*Drew Dickerson is a writer and graduate student in English at UC Berkeley. His writing has been published in* n+1, The Point *,* The Drift *, and* The Onion *. He is at work on a novel.*

items.feedText: Tarnovskaya, Boris S. Tikhonov Tetrameric and pseudo-tetrameric cationic channels, which are targeted by many drugs and toxins, play key roles in the cell physiology and pathophysiology. This diverse superfamily of P-loop channels includes but is not limited to voltage-gated potassium, sodium and calcium channels, TRP channels, and ionotropic glutamate receptors. In hundreds of crystal and cryoEM structures of P-loop channels, the general folding is rather similar but subfamily-specific structural details vary greatly. The latter underlie atomic mechanisms of ion selectivity, gating, sensitivity to drugs and toxins, and dysfunction of thousands disease-associated variants. Understanding these mechanisms may benefit from comparative analyses of multiple structures.
items.articleBody: Tetrameric and pseudo-tetrameric cationic channels, which are targeted by many drugs and toxins, play key roles in the cell physiology and pathophysiology. This diverse superfamily of P-loop channels includes but is not limited to voltage-gated potassium, sodium and calcium channels, TRP channels, and ionotropic glutamate receptors. In hundreds of crystal and cryoEM structures of P-loop channels, the general folding is rather similar but subfamily-specific structural details vary greatly. The latter underlie atomic mechanisms of ion selectivity, gating, sensitivity to drugs and toxins, and dysfunction of thousands disease-associated variants. Understanding these mechanisms may benefit from comparative analyses of multiple structures. Here, we propose a statistical method to reveal structural determinants of folding in related proteins, which involves clustering of residue-residue contact energies. We applied the method to a pH-gated potassium channel KcsA and a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb. Twenty 3D-aligned experimental structures of each channel with universal residue labels were downloaded from database www.plic3da.com and Monte Carlo energy minimized. Residue contact energies clustered in the multidimensional space of contacts automatically discriminated open vs. closed states of KcsA, and wild-type vs. chimeric structures of NavAb. We found and analyzed specific contacts that underlie structural peculiarities. The proposed approach may help detecting folding peculiarities and their structural determinants between subfamilies of P-loop channels, within individual subfamilies, and could be adapted to other proteins.

items.articleBody:
The 61st Venice Biennale, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, concluded yesterday, November 22, reporting 714,015 visitors during its six-month run. Nearly 30,000 visitors attended the pre-opening of *In Minor Keys*, which included a record-high 100 participating countries.

Despite running three weeks shorter than previous editions to allow for the installation of the renovated Central Pavilion at the Giardini, *In Minor Keys* is the second highest-attended exhibition in the event's history. (The 2022 edition holds the record, counting more than 800,000 visitors.) The news follows the highest-ever visitor numbers at the most recent editions of the Venice Architecture Biennale and Venice International Film Festival, two other landmark events organized under the La Biennale di Venezia.

Following [Kouoh's unprecedented death](https://hyperallergic.com/artists-pay-tribute-to-koyo-kouoh-in-poetry-caravan-at-venice-biennale/) in May 2025 at the age of 57, her team of collaborators — Rasha Salti, Marie Hélène Pereira, Gabe Beckhurst Feijoo, Siddhartha Mitter, and Rory Tsapayi — carried out the exhibition of 109 international artists, many of whom hailed from Africa and the Caribbean diasporas.

Wangechi Mutu’s elegant bronze “Simbi Siren” (2026) at the 2026 Venice Biennale (photo Hrag Vartanian/ *Hyperallergic* )

items.articleBody:
*τρία* is the third instalment in **Aeson Zervas’** ongoing sequence for Heat Crimes, continuing the numbering of his untitled pieces from the self-titled debut (1–8), through *Hazlom* (9–17), and now from “Χωρίς τίτλο 18” to “Χωρίς τίτλο 29”. That continuity matters. Zervas’ reclusiveness, the absence of explanatory titles and the progressive numbering make the three albums feel like fragments of one unresolved archive. On *τρία*, Greek folk memory, rebetika, damaged soundtrack music and dubby electronics repeatedly surface and disappear. “Χωρίς τίτλο 20” slips into filmic suspense; “Χωρίς τίτλο 21” gives itself over to rebetika; the almost unbearably melancholic “Χωρίς τίτλο 22” is followed by the repeated scream of “Χωρίς τίτλο 23”; later, “Χωρίς τίτλο 25” places traditional material over an electronic dub framework. The album keeps circling between fairground unease, glitchy tapes, folk citation and invented memory. Is this, as Mark Fisher would have it, a harrowing investigation of memory disorder?

Mark Fisher’s hauntology is an obvious reference point: damaged repetition, obsolete media and sounds that appear to belong to futures that never arrived. [Matt Bluemink](https://shop.becoming.press/products/the-future-is-not-lost-music-technology-and-the-creation-of-worlds-2026-by-matt-bluemink) takes that diagnosis and pushes against its pessimism, arguing that anti-hauntology can use the past as material for new cultural forms rather than remaining trapped in mourning. But the work of Egyptian-born producer [Abadir](https://acloserlisten.com/2026/09/18/abadir-the-primitivist/), whom we interviewed recently, complicates the argument further. Abadir rejects the assumption that “newness” must be tied to an abstract future at all, especially when that future is defined through a Western critical vocabulary. For him, the more interesting question is how the past can be used creatively “without mourning it” while remaining grounded in the present; he is equally suspicious of escaping backwards through nostalgia and forwards through futurism. That position feels particularly useful for *τρία*. Zervas is clearly, but also self-consciously, nostalgic, yet nostalgia here is unstable and frequently unpleasant. Rebetika is not restored as heritage; it is scratched, looped, interrupted, displaced and contaminated by technologies and musical languages from elsewhere.

This also makes the Mediterranean dimension of the record more important than a simple Fisherian reading might allow. Zervas’ Greece is not an isolated national memory but a sedimented space in which Greek, Anatolian, Ottoman, North African and contemporary electronic histories overlap. The idea of Mediterranean music as a form of historical recomposition—taking materials already in circulation and assembling them into new cultural possibilities—fits *τρία* closely. Its imagined past may never have existed, but that does not make it escapist; it can also be a way of refusing a museumised, Eurocentric version of Greek antiquity as suggested by the label notes.

Marc Armand’s cover captures this beautifully. A broken archaeological piece lies on the floor of what appears to be a museum, caught in a shaft of light, while intact artefacts remain displayed on the walls. *τρία* behaves similarly: it removes cultural memory from the wall, breaks chronology and leaves the fragments where they can interfere with the present. The question, then, may not be whether Zervas is producing the music of the future. Abadir is right to make that category suspect. Perhaps the more urgent music now comes from artists for whom neither past nor future offers an easy refuge—artists forced to work inside an unstable present and to make something from whatever histories, technologies and damaged materials remain available.

The album raises many questions that deserve further elaboration. For what it is worth, I personally believe that those making the music of the future today—whatever that might mean—are often those for whom the future is not a given: artists in Ukraine and elsewhere confronting imperialism, war and genocide, and those faced with the very impossibility of the present. ( **Gianmarco Del Re** )

items.articleBody: This study examined the effects of Content-Based Language Teaching (CBLT) on EFL students’ multi-level reading comprehension, focusing on literal, inferential, and critical dimensions. A quasi-experimental design was employed with 60 first-year university students at Mattu University, Ethiopia, divided into experimental and control groups. The experimental group received over an eight-week CBLT intervention using content-based thematic reading materials, while the control group was taught through conventional reading instruction. Data were collected using researcher-developed parallel reading comprehension tests and analyzed using MANOVA, MANCOVA, ANCOVA, and paired-samples t-tests. Results indicated no statistically significant differences between the groups at pretest, confirming baseline equivalence. However, post-intervention findings revealed a significant multivariate effect of CBLT on reading comprehension, p < .001. Follow-up analyses showed significant improvements in literal and inferential comprehension for the experimental group, while the effect on critical comprehension was not statistically significant. The findings showed statistically significant between-group differences favoring the experimental group in literal and inferential comprehension after controlling for pretest scores. However, the difference in critical comprehension was not statistically significant. The study suggests that integrating content and language instruction can strengthen reading development in EFL contexts, although higher-order comprehension development may progress more gradually. Limitations include the relatively small sample size, single-institution setting, and short intervention period, indicating the need for future longitudinal and multi-site research.

items.title: Faurschou Ends Its Public Exhibition Program as Its New York Space Heads for Demolition
items.subtitle: When Faurschou New York opened in 2019, the New York Times compared it to major collector-founded institutions like the Hill Art Foundation, the FL…
items.feedText: But unlike those institutions, Faurschou New York was not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It also never quite lived up to its lofty expectations. items.articleBody:
When Faurschou New York opened in 2019, the *New York Times* compared it to major collector-founded institutions like the Hill Art Foundation, the FLAG Art Foundation, and the Brant Foundation. But unlike those institutions, Faurschou New York was not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It also never quite lived up to its lofty expectations.

In March 2025, Faurschou, which was founded as a private art museum and art consultancy in Copenhagen in 1986, announced that the New York outpost was closed “for renovations.” It never reopened. The Greenpoint building that housed it was sold in June to a developer, city records show, and the city has approved its demolition. A condominium planned for the site cements what founder and art collector Jens Faurschou himself announced in April: After four decades, Faurschou’s public exhibitions are over.

The building at 148-150 Green Street, once home to Faurschou New York and the restaurant Ilis, was sold at the end of June to the developer Investmates for $25.55 million, according to city property records reviewed by *ARTnews*. The seller, Green Art Holdings LLC, bought it in 2017 for $18 million, according to *Commercial Observer*. On October 27, the Department of Buildings approved its full demolition, according to city records. Investmates plans a seven-story, 73-unit condominium on the site, *Crain’s* reported.

In a [statement](https://faurschou.com/journal/closing-remarks) posted to the company’s website, Jens Faurschou said that with the closing of the New York space he was “bringing the public exhibition program to an end.” After 40 years, he wrote, his “direction changes”: He will focus on his family, private dealing, and working with artists, institutions, and collections. The statement does not clarify what will become of the collection, or whether the Copenhagen and Beijing spaces remain operational.

Faurschou staged solo exhibitions of artists from Tracey Emin to Shirin Neshat and Danh Vo, and showed works by Robert Rauschenberg and Louise Bourgeois. Programming at its global locations appeared to have stopped years earlier: Copenhagen last listed an exhibition in 2018 and Beijing in 2021-22, according to the company’s website and exhibition listings.

Its 12,000-square-foot New York space last hosted an exhibition of work by the Chinese artist Ai Weiwei, which ended in February 2025. As of late October 2025, the exhibition appeared to still be installed, visible through the windows. Neither the artist’s studio nor Faurschou responded to a request for comment at that time.

His statement did not address the company’s finances, which have come under scrutiny in recent years. An auditor warned about its accounts, and a court issued a bankruptcy order against Faurschou ApS in November 2025 that was canceled two weeks later.

Jens Faurschou (C) at the Getty Medal Dinner in 2017 at The Morgan Library and Museum in New York City.

A degree of mystery surrounds the Danish art dealer, dubbed the “Don Corleone of art” in a 2016 *[Politiken](https://politiken.dk/magasinet/interview/art5616355/Han-ejer-kunst-for-mange-millioner-»Det-er-filantropi.-Fuldstændig.-Jamen-det-er-det«?srsltid=AfmBOopk-ukfAwoT-pnhpCvhD6_C_zme29C1WxeOEr5aIAvHNJoGmYfr)* profile. By his account, his career began in 1984, the year he traveled to New York City and made his first art deal—a few Fluxus works, sold at the suggestion of Art Library founder Knud Pedersen. That same year, he met his future first wife, Luise Faurschou. The two married in 1985 and soon after opened Galleri Faurschou on Store Strandstræde.

According to the profile, the gallery maintained a small but respectable stable of artists—Christian Lemmerz, Nina Sten-Knudsen, Erik A. Frandsen, and Michael Kvium—while also handling blue-chip works. “I sold Warhol,” he recalled. “I sold Poliakoff, I sold Picasso, lots of Picassos. The biggest deal I made, which was the most fun, was around 2004. It was a package of five Picassos and two Mirós.” In 2012, he and Luise relocated the business to Nordhavn, which he continued to run alone following their divorce.

The Faurschou collection underpins his business, but in interviews, he has declined to specify its scope, value, and exact ownership. In 2016, he compared himself to collectors who “have a showroom and a big collection. And sell something from time to time to be able to buy something else.” He claimed to have purchased a monumental work from Robert Rauschenberg, which he said he would part with only for the Museum of Modern Art in New York. (There is no public record that MoMA owns a Rauschenberg that was sold or donated by Jens Faurschou. However, *Mirthday Man*, a work from the Faurschou collection, was shown in a 2017 Rauschenberg exhibition at MoMA.)

Also listed in his collection are works by Louise Bourgeois, Cai Guo-Qiang, Danh Vo, Shirin Neshat, and Bill Viola, as well as a substantial number of pieces by Ai Weiwei. He told *Politiken* the value of the collection “depends on whether it’s a good or a bad day,” and that he is an art dealer but that he “no longer” runs a gallery that represents artists and sells their works.

A 2024 article in the Danish-language outlet *[Børsen](https://borsen.dk/nyheder/virksomheder/kunsthandler-med-kaempetab-fyrer-ansatte)* described Faurschou’s business model as including a “philanthropic” part, which stages “non-commercial” exhibitions. His philanthropic activities, the report notes, include helping establish the art center and nonprofit organization Copenhagen Contemporary. When he opened his Brooklyn location in 2019, Faurschou told the *New York Times* that he occasionally sells works from his private collection and does consulting work to finance his free exhibitions. According to *Børsen*, however, his business is financed by wealthy, unnamed individuals, who also finance and own the art. In 2025, *Jyllands-Posten* estimated that the collection comprises roughly 400 works.

Faurschou has said that these non-commercial shows have cost him several million DKK over the years. The *Politiken* profile notes that several of Faurschou’s companies narrowly sidestepped going into the red in 2015, after the sale of several properties in Taastrup. The art dealer said he was “absolutely” generating funds from the collection to remedy the shortfall.

*Jyllands-Posten* reported in 2025 that with a loss exceeding DKK 25 million ($3.6 million) in 2024, his holding company, Faurschou Holding ApS, had amassed total losses of nearly DKK 174 million ($25.3 million) since its founding in 2012. Company accounts show equity has been negative for six straight years, standing at a deficit of DKK 154 million ($22.4 million) as of 2024. Given these circumstances, the auditor expressed doubts about the value of the art Faurschou has purchased, noting that there was “significant uncertainty about the valuation of the company’s assets.”

The 2023 accounts were similarly fraught. *Børsen* reported in 2024 that despite his industry renown, “the seasoned art dealer has blood-red accounts, where virtually no values are registered.” Faurschou also had a dispute with an auditor from Deloitte, who at the time questioned his business model. According to the article, the auditor wrote that the company accounts “do not give a true and fair view of the companies’ liabilities, assets and financial position, and in addition, the auditor does not believe in the companies’ future operations.”

The report added: “Because there is no faith in the future operations, the auditor also calls the management report incorrect, as it assumes continued operations.”

This credit history painted a tense backdrop for the company’s brush with bankruptcy. On November 6, 2025, the Probate Court of the Maritime and Commercial Court in Denmark issued a bankruptcy order for Faurschou ApS, only to cancel it on November 20. The cancelation ended the legal process that would have seized the company’s assets and operations, because the legal threshold for bankruptcy was no longer met.

Public records also show legal claims on Faurschou’s own property. [Notices](https://statstidende.dk/messages/S17042026-34) in Statstidende [say](https://statstidende.dk/messages/S17042026-18) Møns Bank asked a court to auction two properties he owns, a house in Humlebæk and a summer house in Nysted, with sales set for May. As of November 23, the land registry still listed him as the owner of the Humlebæk house. Separately, the registry shows the Danish Tax Administration placed liens on that house on April 23 totaling about DKK 8.5 million, or roughly $1.3 million.

For his part, Faurschou had expressed confidence in the future of his company, telling *Børsen* in 2024: “I have tried to explain to the accountant why I see it differently than he does, but I absolutely cannot blame him for what he writes, because the requirements for an accountant are much higher today than they were before.” He said the company was working on “large and complex projects,” the details of which he could not share at the time. He added that, alongside the “philanthropic” part of his business, there was an “income-generating” side, where he acted as a broker for major art dealers and facilitated sales from the company’s collection. His April statement does not indicate whether his plans to focus on private dealing include that brokerage and those collection sales.

Reports have left unclear the exact nature of Faurschou’s operations, and the terms used to describe it have shifted over the years between “foundation” and “private museum.”

“You call [Faurschou] a foundation, but it’s not a trust, is it,” *Politiken* asked. Faurschou replied, “No, but neither is the Tryg Foundation,” referencing the charitable arm of TryghedsGruppen, a Danish holding company that is the largest shareholder of the insurance company Tryg. He confirmed that his business is a limited company and explained that the use of the word “foundation” signals that the art on view is not for sale. Visitors “expect to come into a place where there [are] no sales” being conducted, he said, adding that this also ensured employees at the front desk were not asked about the price list.

When pressed further, he stressed that at least the Copenhagen operation “absolutely” was philanthropic, but did not elaborate on the specifics of the philanthropy. “It’s just that not many people take advantage of the philanthropic offer,” he said.

*The Ozymandias Parade* by Edward Kienholz and Nancy Reddin Kienholz, on view at Faurschou New York in December 2020.

Getty Images

Faurschou launched its Greenpoint, Brooklyn, space in 2019 to great fanfare. Mads Refslund, the Scandinavian chef who cofounded Copenhagen’s Noma with René Redzepi, opened Ilis New York in a space attached to Faurschou. (Refslund is reportedly close with Jens Faurschou and his wife, Marsha, with one source saying he contributed to their wedding menu.) The opening of Ilis, packed with art world regulars, was similarly tasteful: employees’ uniforms were designed by Camilla Staerk and Lady and Butler’s founder Eli Caner. The restaurant closed in May 2026, citing the building’s sale; Refslund told *[Eater](https://eaterny.substack.com/p/one-of-brooklyns-most-striking-restaurants)* that he and a group of investors had tried to buy the building, but were outbid by a developer.

In his closing remark, Jens Faurschou described the whole venture, across four cities, as a “program of cross-cultural dialogue.”

items.articleBody:
While my husband kept his eye on the light plastic kickball wavering indecisively in the air above, his arms upraised to catch it for the out, his feet scuttled side-to-side on the bumpy field, as he tried to position him perfectly. It was his birthday, and we were playing a celebratory game with our extended family at his parents’ house an hour away from ours. After triumphantly catching the ball, he collapsed abruptly to the ground and, when we rushed over, he immediately told me to take him to the ER because he knew a bone had broken. I hate to admit that one of the first things I looked at—silently, selfishly—was which leg was hurt.

Right leg. Driving leg. At that moment, I knew that I was in for what my therapist friend would later call a “growth opportunity.”

Up until that point, my husband had done all of the driving for our family of four, us and our 13-year-old twins; I pinch-hit only when he went out of town. Living previously in Beijing, Brooklyn, and then downtown Boston had obviated most any need to drive, and my skills were basic anyhow, as my immigrant parents had severely limited my mobility as a suburban teenager. In the decade since moving to Cambridge and buying a car, my slight fear of being behind the wheel had deepened into a full-on phobia. The road seemed increasingly like a slippery sheet of ice, unpredictable and dangerous, and I clung to public transit, which is better in Boston than in most American cities though far from comprehensive.

I had always maintained that being terrified to drive in greater Boston was a rational response. Based on accident statistics, Allstate has ranked Boston as America’s worst city for drivers for eleven straight years. There is the running of red lights, the “banging” of “ueys,” the weaving through former-cow-path streets, the traffic jams, the rush hour daredevilry, the cutting off, the honking, the flicking off, the jaywalking, the lawless bicycling, the urgency, the rage, the tailgating. Indeed, it was this last behavior that set me off more than any other. I can picture it now: the heat in my rearview mirror, the voice inside my head that said, *You’re going too fuckin’ slow, you’re a pathetic driver, you need to get out of my way and off the road, you don’t deserve to be here—oh look, an Asian woman, of course.*

Unfortunately, the porous emotional boundaries that had served me well to date as a writer were terrible for a driver. Every time I got behind the wheel, I felt squeezed by the time-is-money capitalist python and crushed down by the country’s sexism and racism; the entire experience of being seen, judged, and honked at was psychologically harrowing. My cringing fear translated into a self-abasing timidity, and I let every single person who wanted to cut in front of me cut. Flash, flash; flash, flash.

After the ER trip that put my husband’s broken fibula in a temporary cast, I managed to pilot the car the hour home on the highway. After his surgery, he was ordered to keep weight off the foot for at least a month, and I prepared to take over the driving. Weekend drum and tennis lessons, weeknight capoeira lessons. I was finally going to learn to drive in Boston.

My instinct on my first drive was to flick loving-kindness at all the other drivers around me as I drove. *May you be happy—and you—and you—and you—and you.* This was a practice I’ve had on and off for the past two decades, ever since I sat my first weeklong silent retreat at the Insight Meditation Society, a loving-kindness focused program led by vipassana teacher Michele McDonald, who counseled us to take a light approach. If you’re sitting on the subway, you can just flick [metta](https://tricycle.org/magazine/metta-practice/) quickly at people, one by one, she said. You don’t have to make it something big and serious. I was living in New York at the time, and it was easy to feel barricaded or hostile or shrunken, especially when crammed into the tin can of the subway with strangers, and flicking loving-kindness at fellow riders shifted something in me—it expanded me, softened me, softened the space between me and others, woke me to the present. When I did the same while driving, it worked similarly, creating a radiant force field through which all the cars moved and related to one another. I could impute positive intentions to drivers I’d read earlier as only erratic, selfish, or terrifying. Even when confronted with impatience and rage, through the practice I learned that those feelings did not have to become mine. Each time I drove, my mind grew quieter.

Of all of the categories of people one can send loving-kindness to (self, benefactor, friend, neutral, difficult), I’ve always found the self the hardest, or at least I’ve found it hard to receive my own good intentions, but in this time of forced growth, I had to try. I returned to the [Metta Bhavana](https://dharmaseed.org/talks/3512/): *May I be safe, may I be peaceful.* In this mindset, when I had to make a turn, I realized that I didn’t have to peel out in front of oncoming traffic in a death-defying manner, no matter what the person behind me insisted. I could simply wait until there was a gap in traffic or someone let me go. And they did. There’s actually a lot of kindness out on the roads, in moments people do seem to understand that we’re suffering through this abominable system together and a little kindness can shift the whole system. These kindnesses, and my own, enabled me to enter the slipstream of humanity as an equal. Before, I used to flash my lights, urging others to turn out of terror, but slowly and through practice, I began to do it mainly to be part of the web of the road. I’ve become more confident about driving exactly how I want; after all, these roads are my roads too. And I admit that on some days I do hit the gas instead of flashing my lights because there are places I need to get to on time too.

In retrospect, I see I used the loving-kindness practice to recreate the conditions of bicycling in China, a practice that also began in terror when I moved there in my early 20s but soon became one of my favorite parts of living there. The crucial difference in the driving cultures is that in China, two decades ago at least, driving was incorrigibly social, with cars and bicycles and pedestrians maintaining an exquisite awareness of the world around them, like stars accommodating one another in a jellied, shifting constellation. By contrast, driving in the U.S. is a deeply antisocial activity, everyone zooming around mindlessly as if they are the sun around which the entire roadway universe should revolve. The Chinese view is closer to the Buddhist one, where we are not individuals full of a separate self-nature but instead are waves in a vast, interdependent ocean of being. Nowhere in the world more vividly demonstrates to me the idea that life arises from innumerable and interconnected causes and conditions beyond our control than the wild roadways of greater Boston.

Nowhere in the world more vividly demonstrates to me the idea that life arises from innumerable and interconnected causes and conditions beyond our control than the wild roadways of greater Boston.

A month after the fibula break, metta had helped me muster up the courage to do the routine drives, but I still hadn’t mastered getting back on the highway or parallel parking or crossing the river into Boston proper, and I still struggled with dread when I was scheduled to drive. Recently, in preparation to fetch my son from a sleepover at his friend’s house during a nor’easter, I tried to give myself a panicked crash course in the confuddling cuneiform of the windshield wipers, but when I pictured accidentally turning on the high beams instead, and subsequently crashing, I allowed myself to chicken out and ask the friend’s dad, a much more experienced driver than I, if he would be willing to drive my son back, and he did.

My husband recently got his cast off and is now in a boot, but the doctor prescribed yet another month of keeping weight off his foot and then another two weeks of walking with the boot, and then we’ll see. The night we found out, I had a nightmare: I was driving a car that was hurtling at top speed down a highway in New Jersey at night, my husband and our best friends in the car, but I was shocked to find myself steering from the middle of the back seat. As I struggled to follow the arcane directions on Google Maps, I yelled out for help to the men in the front seat, only to find that they were both fast asleep. Then I heard my friend next to me hollering at me to stay awake, but I couldn’t, my eyes kept dropping closed, and I could hear car horns faintly through my drowsy haze as the car drifted all over the highway. I jolted awake. I interpret this dream to mean that at this moment, I feel both in control and out of control, which is not a bad description of driving, and of life. While having no power over the mighty ocean, when awash in its convulsions, the wave called “I” does have some choice in how to incline its mind. Before I turn the key each time, I remind myself: flick, flick, flick; flick, flick, flick.

Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

items.articleBody: Classical models of embryonic patterning explain how cells acquire positional identities by responding to different concentration thresholds along morphogen gradients. Yet many developmental systems generate spatial patterns through temporal programs of gene expression, raising the question of how these programs translate into spatial organization. In the short-germ insect Tribolium castaneum, for example, periodic pair-rule gene expression that drives segmentation and nonperiodic gap-gene expression that specifies regional identities emerge sequentially at the posterior and propagate anteriorly as waves. To investigate how these temporal programs give rise to spatial patterns, we developed a sequential multiplexed imaging strategy based on hybridization chain reaction (HCR), allowing us to visualize up to ten anterior-posterior (AP) patterning genes within the same embryo. We combined this approach with intronic-exonic labeling to infer gene-expression dynamics and characterize the propagation of expression domains. Our analysis revealed that gap-gene expression domains remain dynamic and continue to propagate during tissue elongation. To test whether spatial organization preserves the temporal sequence established at the posterior, we compared the temporal order of expression peaks and half-height borders with their relative spatial positions along the AP axis. Primary pair-rule genes generally preserved the expected order, whereas some gap-gene landmarks appeared in a different relative order in space than in time. Together with the continued propagation of gap-gene domains, these findings suggest that their spatial organization does not simply preserve the initial temporal sequence but can change as expression propagates anteriorly. Such differences could arise because gene-expression domains propagate at different speeds, because regulatory interactions between genes change as expression propagates away from the posterior, or both. Our findings therefore suggest that translating time into space involves more than preserving a temporal sequence: the process can also reshape the relationships among gene-expression domains as spatial patterns emerge.

items.articleBody:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.

The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for *The New York Times*, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “[Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/opinion/anthropic-ipo-ai-regulation.html),” and it opens as follows:

“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”

My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported ([including myself](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/opinion/ai-silicon-valley.html)), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like *Less Wrong* and *Overcoming Bias*, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.

This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. [It’s exactly what they believe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jt508VjX2H8).

Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”

As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)

Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.

It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:

“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”

To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.

#### In Other News

For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out [my recent technical article](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-superintelligence-debate) for the *IEEE Spectrum*, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful [AI Alert newsletter](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-alert-signup).)

items.title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul

items.articleBody:
A commuter riding the Metro in Washington, D.C., snapped photos of a man working on a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” Obtained by ProPublica

Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

### Do You Have a Tip for ProPublica?

If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

Send Us a Tip

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s departure as head of the Smithsonian, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

Three Smithsonian museums, dedicated to African American history, American history, and natural history, seen from the Washington Monument Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

As [recounted by ProPublica in September](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-smithsonian-museum-american-history-became-target-trump-culture-war), the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.

The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated, “including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the development that led our nation to where it is today.”

The report was released with symbolic fanfare on the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding. The administration’s announcement of its next move on this front may have less pop, given its soft rollout on the Orange Line.

### Read More

[How the Smithsonian Became the Latest Front in Trump’s Culture War](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-smithsonian-museum-american-history-became-target-trump-culture-war)

items.articleBody:
Indianola, Texas a coastal town that was once the second largest port in Texas next to at the time Galveston.In 1956 the port received a shipment of camels as part of the United States Camel Corps experiment to replace horses and mules as the primary work animal for southwestern America.

During the Civil War, it was occupied by the Union army, once in 1862, then again a year later. Part of that regiment later drowned moving from Indianola to Matagorda island.

The island was later hit twice again, this time by hurricanes, in 1876 and 1886. The second hurricane was accompanied by a major fire and also submerged most of the town, killing hundreds.

Now basically no sign of the town is left other than a few plaques (one being a marker of where the courthouse used to be). It is however valued as a great spot for fishing for local trout, redfish and flounder.

items.articleBody:
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as [The Night Watch](https://www.openculture.com/2020/05/the-largest-most-detailed-photograph-of-rembrandts-the-night-watch-is-now-online-zoom-in-see-every-brush-stroke.html), [Girl with a Pearl Earring](https://www.openculture.com/2021/07/a-gallery-of-1800-super-high-resolution-images-of-classic-paintings.html), and [The Garden of Earthly Delights](https://www.openculture.com/2022/03/a-digital-archive-of-hieronymus-boschs-complete-works.html). But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the *Ghent Altarpiece*, also called the *Adoration of the Mystic Lamb*, by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching [the video from The Gaze](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4APkXceabVY) above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at [the online Ghent Altarpiece](https://closertovaneyck.kikirpa.be/ghentaltarpiece/#home), seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being [the most stolen work of art in history](https://www.openculture.com/2020/12/how-jan-van-eycks-masterpiece-the-ghent-altarpiece-became-the-most-stolen-work-of-art-in-history.html)), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it *in situ* at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

[The Meaning of Hieronymus Bosch’s The Garden of Earthly Delights Explained](https://www.openculture.com/2021/04/the-meaning-of-hieronymus-boschs-the-garden-of-earthly-delights-explained.html)

items.articleBody: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

items.articleBody:
Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt. Elisabeth Waczek vom Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF) erklärt, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation zu einer differenzierten Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung beitragen kann.

**Elisabeth Waczek** ist studierte Philosophin und Referentin für Wissenstransfer am PRIF – Leibniz-Institut für Friedens- und Konfliktforschung. Einer ihrer Schwerpunkte liegt in der Wissenschaftskommunikation des [Clusters Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)](https://www.prif.org/forschung/cntr), an der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit.

**Seit dem russischen Angriff auf die Ukraine wird deutlich intensiver über Sicherheit und militärische Technologien diskutiert. Spüren Sie seit der Gründung Ihres Forschungsclusters 2023 ein wachsendes Interesse an Ihrer Arbeit?**

Wir spüren definitiv ein wachsendes Interesse.

Unser Fokus liegt auf Rüstungskontrolle im weiteren Sinne. Wir beschäftigen uns mit der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit. Zu Beginn habe ich es als eine deutlich größere Herausforderung wahrgenommen, die Relevanz dessen zu erklären. Mittlerweile merke ich: Das haben viele Leute auf dem Schirm. Diese Themen sind stark ins Bewusstsein gerückt. Viele Leute in Europa haben nun das Gefühl, wir müssen uns wieder stärker mit dem Thema Sicherheit auseinandersetzen.

**Ihr Forschungscluster beschäftigt sich mit Technologien, die bestehende Machtverhältnisse verändern könnten. Woran erkennen Sie, dass eine technologische Entwicklung über die Fachcommunity hinaus sicherheitspolitisch relevant wird?**

Unsere Mitarbeitenden aus den Sozialwissenschaften und aus den Natur- und Technikwissenschaften kommen gemeinsam zu einer Einschätzung: Ist das eine Entwicklung, die disruptives Potenzial hat?

Konkret bedeutet das zum Beispiel: Lassen sich neue Technologien oder Forschungsergebnisse missbrauchen, um Waffen herzustellen? Welche Akteur*innen könnten Zugang bekommen, die ihn zuvor nicht hatten? Reicht bestehende Regulierung noch aus, um schädliche – vielleicht auch unbeabsichtigte – Folgen zu minimieren? Gefährlich wird es zum Beispiel, wenn Technologie die Dynamiken so stark beschleunigt, dass deeskalierende Instrumente wie die Rüstungskontrolle nicht mehr Schritt halten können, oder wenn sich nicht mehr feststellen lässt, woher eine Bedrohung kommt.

Interessanterweise kommen unsere Wissenschaftler*innen auch immer wieder zu der Einschätzung, dass dieses disruptive Potenzial gar nicht so dramatisch ist. Oft geht dem viel Hype voraus und besonders reißerische, aber vielleicht eher unwahrscheinliche Szenarien bekommen viel Aufmerksamkeit. Beim Thema KI zum Beispiel. Da ist es Aufgabe der Wissenschaft, erst einmal einen nüchterneren Blick einzunehmen und zu schauen: Wie gefährlich ist das denn wirklich? Welche Anwendungen haben das größte Potenzial negativer Auswirkungen und wo liegen womöglich auch Chancen? Am Ende kommt oft so etwas dabei raus wie: Ja, man muss das Thema ernst nehmen, aber man sollte nicht in Panik verfallen.

**Wenn Sie sich etwas für die gesellschaftliche Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung wünschen könnten: Was sollte die Öffentlichkeit aus Ihrer Sicht besser verstehen, um einen informierten Umgang mit diesen Themen zu ermöglichen?**

### Cluster Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)

Das CNTR am PRIF untersucht, wie neue Technologien und wissenschaftliche Entwicklungen die internationale Sicherheit beeinflussen. Forschende aus verschiedenen Disziplinen analysieren mögliche Risiken und Chancen technologischer Innovationen und entwickeln Empfehlungen, um die internationale Rüstungskontrolle zu stärken.

Ein Beispiel: Ich war auf einer Tagung, bei der die Sprache auf das Thema Dual-Use-Forschung kam. Das sind Forschung oder Technologien, die legitime zivile Anwendungen haben, aber auch in militärischer Weise gebraucht oder in illegitimer Weise missbraucht werden können.

Auf dieser Tagung hat jemand gesagt: „Ist doch ganz klar, Dual-Use-Forschung sollten wir einfach nicht machen.“ Das ist ein häufiges Missverständnis. Mittlerweile haben so viele Forschungsbereiche einen Dual-Use-Charakter, etwa große Teile der Informatik oder Medizin. In der Kommunikation tragen wir die Verantwortung, zu sagen: Nur weil eine Forschung Sicherheitsrisiken in sich trägt, ist diese Forschung nicht automatisch schlecht oder illegitim. Sie kann trotzdem wichtig sein.

Auch bei der Diskussion um Zivilklauseln, die in den letzten Jahren ziemlich intensiv geführt wurde, ist es wichtig, sich vor Augen zu führen, welche Funktion solche Instrumente überhaupt haben. Natürlich ist die Wissenschaftsfreiheit im Grundgesetz verankert. Genauso ist im Grundgesetz verankert, dass man als Forschende*r nicht einfach Massenvernichtungswaffen entwickeln kann. Interessant sind vor allem die Graubereiche, in denen Forschende viel Eigenverantwortung tragen müssen.

Es ist wichtig, dass Forschende mit dieser Verantwortung durch institutionelle Strukturen unterstützt werden. In der Wissenschaftskommunikation tragen wir dazu bei, das Bewusstsein für diese Themen zu schärfen.

**Wie gelingt es, im Diskurs um sicherheitsrelevante Forschung berechtigte Sorgen zu adressieren, ohne zu dramatisieren oder zu verharmlosen?**

Es ist wichtig zu beobachten, mit welchen Vokabeln und Bildsprache der Diskurs stattfindet, und das immer wieder kritisch zu reflektieren. Wir versuchen generell, Darstellungen, die als kriegs- oder gewaltbejahend empfunden werden können, zu vermeiden, ebenso martialische Bildsprache.

Wenn man Kommunikation als Handwerk lernt, bekommt man bestimmte Best Practices mit: wie Menschen Informationen aufnehmen und wie man Gehör findet. Dazu gehören Mittel wie: klare Botschaften, starke Verben, einfache Sätze, die im Gedächtnis bleiben. Wir müssen uns im Wettbewerb um Aufmerksamkeit gegen eine Flut an Desinformationen durchsetzen und brauchen diese Techniken. Aber gleichzeitig entziehen sich wissenschaftliche Inhalte durch die gebotene Nuancierung oft diesen Best-Practice-Leitlinien.

Diese grundlegende Spannung, die man in der Wissenschaftskommunikation immer hat, verstärkt sich im Umfeld sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung noch einmal mehr.

### „Die Kommunikation sicherheitsrelevanter Themen hat jedoch selbst eine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente“

Elisabeth Waczek

**Ihr Forschungscluster vereint naturwissenschaftliche und sozialwissenschaftliche Perspektiven. Wie wirkt sich dieser interdisziplinäre Ansatz auf die Art und Weise, wie Sie Forschungsergebnisse kommunizieren, aus?**

Eine spannende Alltagsbeobachtung für die Wissenschaftskommunikation ist, dass Menschen verschiedene Disziplinen unterschiedlich wahrnehmen. Bei manchen Disziplinen erkennen sie die erforderliche Fachexpertise leichter, bei anderen haben sie das Gefühl, jede*r könne mitreden.

Die Philosophie fällt dem manchmal stärker zum Opfer, weil sie viele Begriffe und Konzepte verwendet, die jeder im Alltag verwendet und kennt. Deswegen gibt es bestimmte Berührungsängste vielleicht weniger als mit der Molekularbiologie oder der Quantenphysik. Politik- und Sozialwissenschaften liegen irgendwo dazwischen. Natürlich hängt das auch davon ab, welche Berührungspunkte man selbst mit den entsprechenden Disziplinen hat. Und wir können beobachten, dass sich das auch verändert. Zum Beispiel in der Corona-Pandemie, als Fachbegriffe aus der Virologie und Epidemiologie plötzlich Einzug in alltägliche Gespräche gehalten haben.

Verschiedene Disziplinen erfordern in der Kommunikation auch unterschiedliche Ansätze. Die sozialwissenschaftlichen Themen muss man manchmal stärker von der alltäglichen Betrachtung wegrücken. Es liegt eine besondere Herausforderung darin, nicht nur zu vermitteln, was die Ergebnisse der Forschung in diesen Bereichen sind, sondern auch zu verdeutlichen: Was können Wissenschaftler*innen zu diesem Thema sagen, was ich als eine Person, die einfach nur Nachrichten schaut, dazu nicht sagen kann? Es geht also auch darum, bei unserem Zielpublikum eine gewisse Scientific Literacy mit aufzubauen. Auf der anderen Seite kann es im naturwissenschaftlichen Bereich wichtiger sein, die Themen näher an die Leute heranzurücken und vom Fachjargon in etwas zu übersetzen, woran sie anknüpfen können.

[Sicherheit & Innovation Alle Beiträge zum Jahresfokus](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/schwerpunkt-sicherheit-innovation/)

Die Interdisziplinarität erfordert dann, diese Ansätze zusammenzubringen. Wir reden gerade ganz allgemein von Wissenschaftskommunikation, aber wir haben natürlich unterschiedliche Zielgruppen, und die haben unterschiedliche Kenntnisstände. Es ist wichtig, sich das bewusst zu machen und eine Art modularen Ansatz zu wählen. Wir überlegen: Was sind die wichtigsten Kernbotschaften? Welche Hintergrundinformationen könnte eine Person brauchen, die nicht im Thema drin ist? Wie können wir visuelle Elemente einsetzen, um die Zugänglichkeit der Themen zu erhöhen?

**Wissenschaft sollte möglichst offen und transparent sein. Wenn es um sicherheitsrelevante Forschung geht, kann Transparenz jedoch auch Risiken bergen. Wo verläuft da die Grenze zwischen Offenheit und verantwortungsvollem Schutz?**

Das ist immer eine Abwägung im Einzelfall. Ich denke, die eigentliche, schwierigere Frage findet nicht erst in der Kommunikation statt, sondern schon früher. Bei einem großen Risikopotenzial ist die Frage grundlegend: Was kann ich davon überhaupt veröffentlichen?

Eine mögliche Maßnahme ist, nur einen Teil der Forschungsergebnisse in einem Journal zu veröffentlichen. Das beißt sich natürlich damit, wie Wissenschaft überhaupt funktioniert. Sie ist eigentlich auf Reproduzierbarkeit, Offenheit und Dialog angelegt. Die Wissenschaftskommunikation kann sich hier nicht gänzlich aus der Affäre ziehen. Allerdings denke ich, dass wir nicht diejenigen sind, die solche Abwägungen treffen können, weil sie selbst Gegenstand einer wissenschaftlichen Einschätzung sind.

Die Kommunikation sicherheitsrelevanter Themen hat jedoch selbst eine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente. Denn dadurch, dass man sagt: „Achtung, diese Forschung ließe sich missbrauchen auf diese und jene Art und Weise“, erzeugt man auch die Gefahr, dass man die Aufmerksamkeit auf das Missbrauchspotenzial lenkt. Auch wir Kommunikator*innen, die Aufmerksamkeit lenken wollen, müssen also umsichtig vorgehen.

items.articleBody:
Berlin, 23. November 2026 – Heute berät der Innenausschuss des Deutschen Bundestags über den Entwurf für das KI-Migrationsverwaltungsgesetz (KIMVG). Mit dem Gesetz soll Migrationsbehörden erlaubt werden, KI-Systeme mit Daten aus Visums- und Asylverfahren entwickeln und einsetzen zu dürfen. Bereits vergangene Woche hat AlgorithmWatch mit 36 weiteren Organisationen einen gemeinsamen Appell unterzeichnet und darin konkrete Nachbesserungen in den Bereichen Datenschutz, Evaluation und Transparenz gefordert. Darüber hinaus kritisiert AlgorithmWatch, dass der jetzige Gesetzentwurf zu vielen Behörden erlaubt, beim Einsatz von KI Grundrechte einzuschränken.

Nora Oppermann, Junior Policy Managerin bei AlgorithmWatch, kommentiert:

„Das KIMVG soll einem kaum begrenzten Behördenkreis ermöglichen, mit hochsensiblen Daten eigene KI-Systeme zu entwickeln. Dazu zählen 225 Auslandsvertretungen, 585 kommunale Ausländerbehörden und sämtliche Dienststellen der Polizei. Zwischen touristischen Visa aus Nordamerika und Asylgesuchen von geflüchteten Menschen aus Kriegs- und Krisengebieten wird dabei kein Unterschied gemacht.

Hinzu kommt, dass das KIMVG einen automatisierten Abgleich von Angaben aus den Anträgen mit öffentlich zugänglichen Daten aus dem Internet erlauben soll, beispielsweise von Social-Media-Plattformen. Dabei handelt es sich um ein Verfahren, das wir sonst nur von Nachrichtendiensten und aus der Strafverfolgung kennen und dessen Nutzen aufgrund seiner Anfälligkeit für Fehler und gefälschte Daten stark umstritten ist. Antragstellende werden so nicht nur für intransparente KI-Experimente ausgenutzt, sondern zudem unzuverlässigen automatisierten Entscheidungen ausgesetzt.

Ohne Vorgaben für eine Begrenzung des Einsatzes, die Qualität der Daten, eine unabhängige Kontrolle der Systeme und strikte Transparenz droht der Einsatz von KI im Migrationsbereich zu einem undurchsichtigen und diskriminierenden Fiasko zu werden.“

items.articleBody:
arXiv:2611.26663v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.
