## One of Van Gogh’s Final Paintings Just Sold for a Record-Breaking $190 Million

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/van-gogh-blossoming-chestnut-trees-sale-sothebys/)

“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) by Vincent van Gogh, 1890. (Photo: courtesy of Sotheby’s)

A painting by [Vincent van Gogh](https://mymodernmet.com/vincent-van-gogh-photograph/) has sold for a record-breaking $190.4 million at [Sotheby’s](https://www.sothebys.com/en/) in New York, making it the most expensive work by the artist to ever sell at auction. The painting, titled *Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees)*, was completed just two months before Van Gogh’s death in 1890. However, in the days leading up to the auction, the painting became the subject of a dispute surrounding its ownership during the Nazi era.

Van Gogh painted *Blossoming Chestnut Trees* on May 24, 1890, just days after arriving in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise following his stay at a psychiatric hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The painting depicts people walking along a street lined with blossoming chestnut trees, which Van Gogh captured using his signature bold brushstrokes and vibrant colors. Despite being one of the last works he ever completed, the painting had been held in a private collection for decades.

The piece belonged to the Argentine Blaquier-Arrieta family since 1975, but its ownership history goes back much further. In 1909, the painting was purchased by Samuel Fischer, a prominent German Jewish publisher. Following his death in 1934, the painting remained in the family until it was sold in 1936, during a period of increasing Nazi persecution of Jewish people in Germany.

Just days before the painting was set to go to auction, descendants of Fischer and his wife, Hedwig, called for the sale to be postponed. The family raised concerns about the circumstances surrounding the painting’s sale in 1936, questioning whether their relatives had been forced to part with it due to Nazi persecution.

However, just one day before the auction, Sotheby’s announced that the Fischer descendants and the painting’s current owners had reached an agreement, allowing the sale to move forward. While the details of the agreement have not been made public, the Fischer family expressed their appreciation for the discussions and for the acknowledgment of their family’s suffering during the Holocaust.

The painting ultimately sold for $165 million, with auction fees bringing the total to $190.4 million. This surpassed the previous auction record for a Van Gogh painting, which was set in 2022 when *Verger avec cyprès* ( *Orchard with Cypresses* ) sold for $117.2 million at Christie’s.

Interestingly enough, [Van Gogh experienced very little commercial success](https://mymodernmet.com/vincent-van-gogh-life/) during his lifetime. Now, more than 130 years after his death, one of his final paintings has become his most expensive work ever sold at auction. And considering that *Blossoming Chestnut Trees* had been privately owned for so long, the sale also marks a rare opportunity for the public to get a closer look at a lesser-known work by one of the world’s most famous artists.

## Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold for a record-breaking $190.4 million at Sotheby’s in New York, after a dispute regarding its storied past.

“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) by Vincent van Gogh, 1890. (Photo: courtesy of Sotheby’s)

items.articleBody:
In my usual summaries of cultural drift, I describe key parameters that have been going bad in the last few centuries re the evolution of cultures. Here I mention 3:

> A few centuries ago… the world had 100Ks of peasant cultures, most facing frequent wars, pandemics, and famines, in an economy that took a millennia to double. But then we merged peasants into a hundred or so national cultures, and then those into just a few world cultures, all of which got so rich, healthy and peaceful that they almost never die. Also, the world economy now doubles every twenty years, fifty times faster than before. So now we are likely in trouble. Every cultural feature has a min scale at which it can vary; below that scale, people have to do it the same. We are doing fine re features that can vary at small scales, but in trouble re features that set game-theoretic equilibria, and so can only vary at large scales. ( [↗ overcomingbias.com](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/five-slogans-re-cultural-drift) )

The other param I usually mention is the fluctuation rate. While centuries ago peasant cultures were quite conservative, trying not to change, we moderns give our highest status to cultural activists who successfully cause big changes to culture. Alas such changes do not usually much promote adaption.

However there are other relevant parameters. The recent cut in global variety is due to many features of culture moving up to larger scales, some to near global scales. But, as many cultural features remain set at smaller scales, like corporate cultures set at firm scales, fewer cultural features are being set at these largest scales. And thus the scope of cultures at our largest scales is declining. *Cultural scope* is another key parameter.

In addition, while the structure of most practices of ancient peasants were set by their culture, and hard to change, in the modern world we allow and even expect great change and variation in most tech and business practices. This limits the scope of modern cultures even more. And cultural drift in a culture of smaller scope is drift in a lower-dimensional space, and so probably less severe.

This suggests another at least partial fix to cultural drift: further cut cultural scope, i.e., how many aspects of our behavior are set by culture, and so hard to vary locally.

One way to cut the scope of culture would be to rely less on prestige in key social institutions like medicine, law, academia, etc. I’ve made many proposals along these lines, which could greatly improve such areas of life. Alas, our world is far more tolerant of innovations in physical arrangements, relative to social arrangements.

This has been a key fact of my life. I started out in physics and computer science, where I noticed that the world eagerly sought even minor innovations. Which were hard to find, as so many sought them. Then when I got into social science I noticed that it seemed far easier to innovate there. I figured I must be especially good at this, but didn’t realize that it is easy for many to find social innovations, as the world mostly just doesn’t adopt the social innovations that people find.

While it doesn’t at all seem crazy that we might be able to further reduce the scope of our largest-scale cultures, we just don’t understand very well what determines such scope, or what has enable many big prior cuts in such scope. But work to figure this out might pay big dividends.

items.articleBody:
A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project "demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery".

Floor plans

Previous

Next

Floor plans

Close

Ground floor plan

Second floor plan

Third floor plan

Fourth floor plan

Typical maisonette floor plan

Typical three-bedroom floor plan

Typical floor plan

"Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design," HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

"We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe," he continued.

"Together, the two phases have delivered the UK's largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK."

More photographs

Previous

Next

More photographs

Close

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development's green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

"A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place," said Bayliss.

"Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context."

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

"We hope residents feel proud to live here," Bayliss concluded.

"Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community," he said.

Read:

HTA Design builds "world's tallest modular housing scheme" in Croydon

"Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood."

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is "leading the way nationally on council home building".

"The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we're achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country," he said.

"We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future."

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) announced the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year's Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

items.articleBody: Background: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for health information and emotional support, yet little is known about their use for mental health by university students, a population with high digital literacy and elevated mental health need. Objective: To estimate the prevalence of GenAI use for mental health support among respondents to a survey at a single UK university and to identify demographic and well-being characteristics associated with use. Methods: Cross-sectional online survey of students at a large UK university. The primary outcome was self-reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. Well-being was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. Associations were examined using multivariable modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios. Results: Of 22,207 students invited, 2020 responded (response rate 9.1%). Among respondents, 25.0% (n=503) reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. The most common reasons were advice when emotionally distressed (n=380, 19.3%), insights into mental health (n=256, 12.7%), and using GenAI as a personal therapist or coach (n=173, 8.6%); 2.7% (n=54) reported using GenAI to seek support when experiencing thoughts of self-harm. Use was more common among students aged 26-29 years, those identifying as Asian, students reporting a declared disability, students enrolled in management programs, and those with lower well-being. Conclusions: Among respondents at a UK university, approximately one in four reported using GenAI for mental health support. Use was concentrated among students reporting poorer well-being and disability, suggesting that GenAI may function as an informal help-seeking pathway. Universities and health services should anticipate GenAI as a help-seeking pathway and ensure appropriate guidance, integration with existing services, and safeguards to support safe and equitable use.

items.articleBody: ObjectiveTo report two cases of insulinoma-related hypoglycemia presenting with seizure-like episodes and to describe the dynamic quantitative electroencephalographic changes during hypoglycemic episodes.MethodsWe retrospectively reviewed the clinical, video-EEG, and imaging data of two patients. Sliding-window qEEG analysis was performed to evaluate spectral changes during hypoglycemic episodes and before and after glucose administration.ResultsBoth patients experienced recurrent early-morning episodes of altered consciousness and abnormal limb movements. Antiseizure medications were ineffective, whereas glucose administration improved both clinical symptoms and EEG abnormalities. In Patient 1, EEG recording demonstrated a transition from a stable background rhythm to diffuse EEG slowing. During episode-related stages, relative alpha and beta power decreased, whereas relative delta power and the theta-to-alpha ratio increased. In Patient 2, EEG slowing was already present when the recording began. During the later recording period, relative alpha power increased, and the delta-to-alpha ratio and slow-wave index decreased, whereas relative delta power did not show a consistent decline. Imaging showed hypervascular pancreatic nodules in both patients. Postoperative histopathology confirmed pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors in both patients.ConclusionInsulinoma-related hypoglycemia can present as seizure-like episodes. Blood glucose measurement during an episode is essential. Dynamic qEEG may help characterize hypoglycemia-related EEG slowing and its changes after intervention.

items.articleBody: Sensory hair cells convert sound-induced vibrations into electrical signals through a process called mechano-electrical transduction (MET). While the protein components of the MET complex are well studied, increasing evidence indicates that MET channel properties are significantly modulated by the surrounding lipid bilayer. The asymmetric distribution of membrane lipids between the inner and outer membrane leaflets is well established to shape membrane mechanics. The recent discovery that the core MET components TMC1 and TMC2 also act as lipid scramblases suggests a direct role for membrane lipid asymmetry in the dynamic shaping of auditory transduction. Because scramblase activity of TMC1/2 disrupts lipid asymmetry, we hypothesized that an opposing flippase may be required to restore and maintain lipid asymmetry. Here, we identify the P4-ATPase ATP8B1 and its chaperone TMEM30B as selectively expressed in mouse outer hair cells (OHCs), enriched in stereocilia, and upregulated following the onset of MET and hearing. Loss of either protein results in elevated auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization, and rapid hair-cell degeneration, demonstrating that lipid homeostasis is crucial for OHC survival. Together, these findings establish ATP8B1 and TMEM30B as key regulators of membrane lipid asymmetry in sensory hair cells and establish TMEM30B as a novel deafness gene.

items.articleBody:
## SABO PROJECT RENOVATES APARTMENT in New York’s LOWER EAST SIDE

Located in **[New York’s](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-new-york/)**Lower East Side, Soft Division is the**[renovation](https://www.designboom.com/tag/renovation-architecture-and-design/)**of a compact**[apartment](https://www.designboom.com/tag/residential-architecture-interiors/)**for a family of three designed by**[SABO project](https://www.designboom.com/tag/sabo-project/)**. Stripped back to its core structure, the residence is organized as a central living space that extends outward into surrounding alcoves. Rounded partitions pass beneath exposed structural steel beams to soften spatial boundaries and establish continuous visual flow between zones. Extending the interior footprint outdoors, a continuous built-in bench runs from the main living area into a compact terrace enclosed with**[steel](https://www.designboom.com/tag/steel/)**mesh and light-filtering**[fabric](https://www.designboom.com/tag/textile-and-fabric-art/)**.

the apartment balances the rough materiality with soft fabric textures | all images [©SABO project](https://sabo-project.com/)

## ROUNDED PARTITIONS AND EXPOSED STEEL form apartment’s interior

Across the interior, raw structural elements, including exposed concrete masonry blocks and mechanical ductwork, are balanced by soft tactile textiles such as bespoke curtains, window shades, and rugs. **[Design studio](https://sabo-project.com/)** SABO project introduces custom curtains featuring large-scale graphic compositions to delineate individual rooms without rigid walls. The bathroom is fully clad in ceramic tiles of varying dimensions arranged to create a continuous tonal gradient.

bold geometric shapes serve as graphic elements as much as tools to organize the space

simple geometries and the use of a single color are repeated throughout all spaces

partitions are rounded to allow one area to flow into the next

taking its cue from the existing wall, a long bench is assembled from masonry blocks

rounded partitions slip beneath structural steel beams

a long bench extends from the living room towards the balcony

the kitchen cabinetry and countertop echo the olive-green beam in the main living space

the kitchen is very tightly packed with concealed storage, appliances, and air conditioning

the small outdoor space is organized around a custom printed curtain

concrete blocks can be stacked and rearranged into stools, tables, and display shelving

the bathroom is wrapped in a pattern of tiles of varying sizes, creating a green grout gradient

**project info:**

**name:** Soft Division

**architect:** [SABO project](https://sabo-project.com/) | [@sabo_project](https://www.instagram.com/sabo_project)

**location:** Lower East Side, New York

**area:** 68 sqm

items.articleBody: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI), a prevalent long-term stroke sequela worldwide, hinders neurological recovery and elevates mortality. Monotherapy with cholinesterase inhibitors yields modest benefits accompanied by adverse effects, creating demand for integrated therapies. Mounting studies indicate that microbiota–gut–brain axis (MGBA) disruption and brain network dysfunction contribute to PSCI. Nevertheless, the causal association between gut microbiota dyshomeostasis and central neural network remodelling, as well as the underlying mechanisms of acupuncture, are not fully clarified. Based on literature from PubMed, Web of Science and CNKI published between 2010 and 2026, this review puts forward a hypothesis: acupuncture ameliorates PSCI via a sequential pathway centred on the MGBA, which restores gut microbiota homeostasis, mediates gut–brain signalling and remodels dynamic brain networks. Evidence from diverse clinical and preclinical works supports separate segments of this pathway, yet the complete causal cascade remains unproven. This model conceptualises PSCI as a central-peripheral coupling disorder driven by cerebral injury, gut dysbiosis, immune-inflammation and brain network failure, where gut microbial disturbance may initiate this pathological cycle. Post-stroke gut dysbiosis can induce microglial M1 polarisation and damage core cognitive networks, likely via short-chain fatty acid reduction, intestinal barrier leakage and abnormal vagal transmission. Acupuncture can reshape gut microbiota, preserve intestinal tight junctions and trigger cholinergic anti-inflammatory responses, but its MGBA-dependent modulation of brain network activity needs further verification. This integrative framework interprets acupuncture’s regulatory effects, connects peripheral and central mechanisms, and supplies theoretical support for future acupuncture research on PSCI.

items.articleBody: Slow waves are a hallmark of sleep homeostasis and a target for enhancing restorative sleep. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) can non-invasively deliver a low-frequency envelope to deep targets and has been shown to increase spectral slow-wave activity during sleep. It remains untested whether tTIS also alters discrete slow waves, how their cortical expression changes, and whether the field each brain receives relates to the response. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, 32 participants received 1 Hz tTIS and 11 a carrier-only control in 3-min episodes targeting the left insula/ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Combining high-density electroencephalography (EEG), source reconstruction and individualized field modeling, we found that tTIS increased slow-wave density by about 20% during and 30% after stimulation, across shallow and deep waves, with limited morphology change. The carrier-only control showed no detected density change. In source space, each wave involved more cortex in both arms, while wave origins did not change. A dose-response analysis showed that tTIS participants who received a stronger modeled field shifted further toward N3 sleep during stimulation, a relation not seen in the control. These results support tTIS as a candidate EEG-compatible tool for modulating slow waves and motivate individualized field modeling to interpret its effects.

items.articleBody:
Kaum ein Abiturthema zeigt so deutlich wie dieses, dass es ihn gibt: einen modernen Deutschunterricht, der die Aufgabe ernst nimmt, jungen Menschen Orientierung in einer digitalen Gesellschaft zu ermöglichen. Ein Kommentar.

Es gibt Abiturthemen, bei denen man als Lehrkraft erst einmal Überzeugungsarbeit leisten muss. Bei denen man vor einem Kurs steht und begründen muss, warum es sich lohnt, sich mit etwas zu beschäftigen, das auf den ersten Blick weit weg ist vom eigenen Leben. Ich habe solche Stunden oft genug gehalten. Und ich habe auf diesem Blog auch schon [dafür gestritten, dass man sie halten sollte.](https://bobblume.de/2019/10/06/diskussion-sollte-goethes-faust-teil-des-lehrplans-sein/)

„Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ gehört nicht dazu. Der sperrige Titel täuscht. Denn worum es hier geht, tragen die Schülerinnen und Schüler jeden Tag in der Hosentasche mit sich herum.

## Wo das Thema im Abitur 2027 eine Rolle spielt

In Nordrhein-Westfalen, Berlin und Brandenburg, Hessen, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein ist das Themenfeld im Abitur 2027 ausdrücklich als Schwerpunkt ausgewiesen, mit leicht unterschiedlichen Akzenten. Mal geht es um politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation zwischen Verständigung und Strategie, mal um den Sprachgebrauch in unterschiedlichen Medien, mal um Rhetorik und Medienwandel. In den übrigen Ländern, etwa in Baden-Württemberg und Bayern, sind genau die Aufgabenformate gefragt, an denen sich das Thema hervorragend üben lässt: die Analyse pragmatischer Texte, die Erörterung und das materialgestützte Schreiben.

Mit anderen Worten: Es ist eines der zentralen Felder des Deutschabiturs.

## Worum es eigentlich geht

Wie wird Sprache eingesetzt, um zu überzeugen, zu mobilisieren, auszugrenzen? Wo legt jemand seine Gründe offen, und wo will er bloß wirken? Diese Fragen konnte man früher an Bundestagsreden und Leitartikeln stellen. Das fällt nicht weg, aber es kommt auch etwas hinzu: Die politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation, die Jugendliche tatsächlich erreicht, hat nochmals völlig andere Formen und Kanäle: ein KI-generiertes Video, das Empörung erzeugt und am Ende einen Shop verlinkt. Ein [Finanzpodcast, der von „Systemmedien“](https://www.t-online.de/leben/kolumne-bob-blume/id_100330412/finanz-influencer-und-podcasts-werden-jugendliche-zum-rechtsruck-verleitet-.html) spricht und damit mehr transportiert als eine Meinung. Eine Kommentarspalte, in der niemand den Text gelesen hat, über den alle streiten. Ein Feed, in dem auf das Kriegsvideo der Tanzclip folgt.

Das ist politische Sprache. Nur eben nicht mehr im Plenarsaal, sondern zwischen zwei Wischbewegungen. Und wer diese Sprache nicht durchschaut, wird von ihr beeinflusst oder [im schlimmsten Fall manipuliert.](https://substack.com/@netzlehrer/p-211289258)

## Kein Entweder-oder

Nun könnte man einwenden, das sei die übliche Anbiederung an die Lebenswelt. Ein bisschen TikTok, damit es sich zeitgemäß anfühlt. Den Einwand muss man ernst nehmen, ich habe ihn selbst oft genug erhoben. An anderer Stelle habe ich beschrieben, dass Deutschunterricht auf [drei Ebenen zur Teilhabe an Kultur](https://bobblume.de/2021/05/31/diskussion-was-soll-und-kann-deutschunterricht/) befähigt: durch basale Grundfertigkeiten, durch die Auseinandersetzung mit Alltagskultur und durch die Hochkultur. Die mittlere Ebene ist diejenige, die sich am schnellsten verändert. Gerade deshalb darf man sie nicht dem Zufall überlassen.

Und es geht nicht um ein Entweder-oder. Wer Kleist liest, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache vor Gericht. Wer ein Empörungsvideo analysiert, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache im Feed. Beides schärft denselben Blick. In der Diskussion um den Faust habe ich geschrieben, dass man Kompetenzen an unterschiedlichen Inhalten lernen kann, aber nur an bestimmten Inhalten unterschiedliche Kompetenzen. Die Sprache der digitalen Öffentlichkeit ist ein solcher Inhalt. An ihr lernt man zu analysieren, zu urteilen und selbst zu schreiben. Und nebenbei etwas, das in keinem Erwartungshorizont steht: den Schritt zurück.

## Fazit

Man kann lange darüber streiten, wie viel Gegenwart der Deutschunterricht verträgt. Bei diesem Thema muss man es nicht. Wenn Schule der Ort sein soll, an dem junge Menschen lernen, sich in der Welt zu orientieren, dann muss sie sich mit der Sprache beschäftigen, in der diese Welt heute verhandelt wird. Nicht obwohl sie den Schülerinnen und Schülern so nah ist, sondern weil sie es ist. Relevanz ist hier kein Zugeständnis an die Jugend. Sie ist der Grund, warum das Thema in die Schule gehört.

## In eigener Sache

Vielleicht ist es euch aufgefallen: Auf diesem Blog war es in letzter Zeit ruhiger. Das liegt nicht daran, dass mir die Themen ausgegangen wären, sondern daran, dass ich vor allem auf Substack schreibe. Dort erscheint jeden Samstag mein Newsletter „Stimme für Bildungswandel“, mit Kommentaren zu Bildungsthemen, Gesprächen und regelmäßig auch mit Material für den Unterricht. Wenn ihr mögt, schaut dort gern vorbei. Die Anmeldung ist kostenlos.
items.body: Ein Kommentar. Es gibt Abiturthemen, bei denen man als Lehrkraft erst einmal Überzeugungsarbeit leisten muss. Bei denen man vor einem Kurs steht und begründen muss, warum es sich lohnt, sich mit etwas zu beschäftigen, das auf den ersten Blick weit weg ist vom eigenen Leben. Ich habe solche Stunden oft genug gehalten. Und ich habe auf diesem Blog auch schon dafür gestritten, dass man sie halten sollte. „Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ gehört nicht dazu. Der sperrige Titel täusch…

items.articleBody: Contemporary large-scale neural recordings have made it possible to answer long-standing questions about the nature of neural activity that gives rise to working memory. In the primate brain, persistent activity in the lateral prefrontal cortex and connected brain areas represents the core neural correlate of working memory, with neurons maintaining elevated firing rates during memory delays through recurrent excitation and glutamate receptor–dependent feedback loops. A key refinement is recognizing that working memory representations can persist at the population level when individual neurons show asynchronous, intermittent, or dynamic activity. We refer to this view as a hybrid attractor, in which recurrent dynamics provide a stable landscape of states while stochastic spiking, synaptic plasticity, and changing neuronal recruitment across time determine how that landscape is occupied and read out. Although activity of populations of neurons is often discussed in abstract terms, a canonical microcircuit composed of pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneuron subtypes, including parvalbumin-positive, somatostatin-positive, and vasoactive intestinal peptide-positive neurons, supports recurrent excitation and precise inhibitory control. The collective firing of such diverse neuron populations gives rise to a rich and dynamic representation of stimulus information in working memory.

items.articleBody:
The surprising benefit of a common enemy

Sallust’s Theorem is that fear of an external enemy promotes internal social unity.

Perhaps more pertinent is the other side of Sallust’s Theorem: the absence or removal of an external enemy leads to internal moral decay and conflict.

Sallust, or more fully Gaius Sallustius Crispus, was a Roman historian and politician around the time of Julius Caesar. Remarkably, several of his works have remained intact to be read over 2000 years later.

Sallust describes unity in the face of common enemies and decline in their absence at several points in the history of Rome’s Republic. His strongest example is the fear of Carthage.

Here’s Sallust in his work The War with Jugurtha, chapter 41 (Latin terms included):

“…before the destruction of Carthage the people and senate of Rome together governed the republic peacefully and with moderation. There was no strife among the citizens either for glory or for power; fear of the enemy (metus hostilis) preserved the good morals of the state.

But when the minds of the people were relieved of that dread (formido), wantonness and arrogance naturally arose, vices which are fostered by prosperity. Thus the peace for which they had longed in time of adversity, after they had gained it proved to be more cruel and bitter than adversity itself.

For the nobles began to abuse their position (dignitas) and the people their liberty (libertas), and every man for himself robbed, pillaged and plundered. Thus the community was split into two parties, and between those the state (res publica) was torn to pieces.” (quoted from Neal Wood, see below)

Sallust sees Rome’s rise and decline as a psychological progression from liberty through glory and ambition to avarice (greed).

You may remember Carthage from the Colosseum scene in the film Gladiator, where Maximus is forced to represent the Carthaginians in Rome’s great victory at the “Battle of Carthage.” It doesn’t go to plan.

Tim Marshall introduced me to Sallust’s Theorem in his fascinating and relevant book Prisoners of Geography. He summarises Sallust’s idea in terms of alliances: “alliances are only strong with the fear of a common enemy.”

In some ways, Sallust’s Theorem is about the danger of getting what we want. We may resent a demanding boss, a fierce local rival, a struggle to build ourselves up from nothing, or a powerful business competitor, yet find that they gave us purpose and brought out the best in us as a group. We can miss them when they’re gone.

—

I believe the term Sallust’s Theorem was introduced by Neal Wood in Wood, N. (1995). Sallust’s Theorem: A Comment on “Fear” in Western Political Thought. History of Political Thought, 16(2), 174–189.

items.title: AI people are very, very, very, very rich

items.articleBody:
As you may have heard, Anthropic had its IPO this past Thursday. At a valuation of $1.5 trillion, it was actually just the second most valuable IPO in history, just behind SpaceX at $1.77 trillion. I bought some shares on the first day at what I thought was a reasonable price, only to see my shares drop the following day as the company’s valuation fell to $1.175 trillion, making it only [the 14th most valuable company](https://companiesmarketcap.com/) in the world. Such are the risks of buying individual stocks!

But that price drop doesn’t change the fact that Anthropic’s IPO was a staggeringly large wealth creation event. Anthropic began hiring lots of employees just a few years ago; now, almost all of those people have either hundreds of millions of dollars, or tens of millions of dollars. Andrew Benson had a good breakdown of exactly who would get what, if the company hit its initial valuation target of $2 trillion:

> Who actually gets rich if Anthropic lists at $2 trillion?…
> - $199B for the 7 controlling co-founders, about 10%
> - $28B for Ben Mann, if his stake matches theirs
> - $100B for the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, 5%
> - $331B in employee options and RSUs, about 17%, That pool covers about 5,300 employees, an average of $62M each…
> [H]ere is roughly how many people made what at $2T:
> - $110M to $400M each: ~300 to 500 people hired by 2023
> - $200M to $300M each: ~440 to 640 hired in 2024
> - $70M to $95M each: ~1,360 hired in 2025
> - $10M to $20M each: ~3,000 hired in 2026
> So about 940 people hired by the end of 2024 average nine figures. Everyone hired since averages eight figures.

The company’s (fully diluted) valuation is now only about 80% of that $2T number, so you have to scale those numbers down a little bit. But it’s still a staggering amount of money for just a few years of work! We’re used to seeing the first few employees at a generational company make hundreds of millions of dollars, but seeing several *hundred* people make that much is just unprecedented.

Let’s put these numbers in perspective. If Anthropic were worth $2T, it would have more centimillionaires than the entire city of Los Angeles. Even with only 350-400 centimillionaires, that’s about as many as Houston, Dallas, and Austin combined:

Source: [Steve Rattner](https://x.com/SteveRattner/status/2123523070044356875?s=19)

Of course, just looking at these numbers tremendously understates the amount of wealth that has been created in the AI industry over the last couple of years. There’s also OpenAI, which is [targeting](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/anthropic-vs-openai-the-financial-metrics-behind-the-ai-battle-4f5b90c0) an IPO valuation of $1.25 trillion. And there are quite a number of AI startups that have gotten very valuable, very quickly. Just a few include Isomorphic Labs at ~$50 billion, Cognition at $48 billion, Prometheus at $41 billion, Safe Superintelligence at $32 billion, VAST Data at $30 billion, Reflection AI at ~$27.5 billion, Cohere at $25.5 billion, ElevenLabs at $22 billion, and so on.

And of course, all of this is just *today*. I wouldn’t have bought Anthropic stock unless I thought the company had a very good chance of becoming much *more* valuable than it is today. Despite the early price drop, I’m still very bullish. I think AI’s extremely cross-domain capabilities mean that Anthropic has a good shot at being a very large, diversified conglomerate:

Furthermore, I think the company is amassing a huge pool of top human talent, essentially giving them a hedge against a future in which AI continues to be a complement to top human talent rather than a substitute. Almost every smart person I know here in Silicon Valley either works there or has strongly considered working there. That makes Anthropic resemble Google back in 2004, which became a legendary brain trust. If anyone can figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI, it’s probably Anthropic. And yes, someone *will* figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI. Even if that means the company only becomes as valuable as [Google or Microsoft is today](https://companiesmarketcap.com/), that means I’ll more than double my own investment.

If that happens, all of those wealth numbers from the top of this post will also more than double. And if the U.S. economy grows robustly and AI itself grows rapidly as a percentage of that economy, this could easily turn out to be the greatest wealth creation event in American history, by far — greater than the internet, far greater than crypto, greater even than the railroads.

I can definitely feel this wealth all around me. A lot of the people I went to potlucks with three years ago now have an order of magnitude more money than anyone I ever met before I turned 30. Some of those people are under 30 themselves. A few of them are billionaires. Now, when I go to house parties, they’re often in lavish designer-furnished mansions overlooking spectacular ocean views from high up on San Francisco hilltops.

As a social phenomenon, this is totally unprecedented. Sarah Chieng [writes](https://x.com/MilksandMatcha/status/2114768311468871731):

> You can build a startup in 9 months, get acquired (but rly acquihired) by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Cognition, and walk away a multi-millionaire…You can join the right company at 22 and become effectively post-economic…And I don't think we've even begun to grapple with the degree to which this is warping an entire generation's relationship with money, ambition, work, and success…When your peers are making generational wealth before 25, what does a normal career even look like anymore[?]

I’m happy for my friends, of course. And I am not personally bothered by seeing displays of great wealth. But I find myself wondering what this is going to do to my society. If the AI class are the *only* people who get rich going forward, what kind of tensions will that produce among the country’s elites? What would it mean for America if wealth inequality goes up far further even than it already has?

#### What if only the AI people get rich?

items.articleBody:
### “This fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet.”

Perhaps the gravest violence we can do to ourselves is to live out our lives believing the world to be a fixity handed down to us by the authorities of history and life to be a matter of taking immutable givens. Daring to believe otherwise — to believe that even our smallest purposeful action alters the monolith of reality in some subtle, meaningful way — is an act of courage and resistance, an act of immense vulnerability to the possibility of disappointment, vulnerability the commonest cowering from which is cynicism.

James Baldwin knew this when he issued his lyrical and impassioned insistence that [“nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/05/21/nothing-is-fixed-james-baldwin-morley-music/) that [“we made the world we’re living in and we have to make it over.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/09/james-baldwin-freedom/)

Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered [how we invent ourselves and reinvent the world](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/17/hannah-arendt-human-condition-speech-action/), observing that “the smallest act in the most limited circumstances bears the seed of boundlessness, because one deed, and sometimes one word, suffices to change every constellation.”

Art by [Dorothy Lathrop](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/03/09/dorothy-lathrop-down-adown-derry/), 1922. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/art-by-dorothy-lathrop-for-down-adown-derry-by-walter-de-la-mare-19224642772_print?curator=brainpicker) and [as stationery cards](https://society6.com/product/art-by-dorothy-lathrop-for-down-adown-derry-by-walter-de-la-mare-19224642772_cards?curator=brainpicker).)

**Richard Powers** knew this when he made his contribution to [Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two](http://www.amazon.com/Take-My-Advice-Letters-Generation/dp/1416578358/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/take-my-advice-letters-to-the-next-generation-from-people-who-know-a-thing-or-two/oclc/49322746&referer=brief_results)) — artist and writer James L. Harmon’s wonderful 2002 anthology of [wisdom from stellar minds](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/10/12/martha-nussbaum-take-my-advice/), a decade in the constellating, envisioned as an eclectic contemporary counterpart to Rilke’s timeless [Letters to a Young Poet](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/06/29/rilke-letters-to-a-young-poet-macy-barrows/), which had moved Harmon deeply when he first encountered it as a young man.

Two decades before Powers won the Pulitzer Prize for his sylvan symphony [The Overstory](https://www.amazon.com/Overstory-Novel-Richard-Powers/dp/039335668X/?tag=braipick-20), he echoes Seamus Heaney’s exhortation to [always remain “true to your own secret knowledge”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/01/19/seamus-heaney-commencement/) and writes:

> Never forget what you were born knowing. That this fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet. Buy the plot some time.

19th-century [Solar System quilt](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/12/06/ellen-harding-baker-solar-system-quilt/) by Ellen Harding Baker, embroidered over the course of seven years as a teaching tool in an era when women were barred from higher education in science and a fraction of the presently known Solar System objects were known. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/solar-system-quilt-by-ellen-harding-baker-1886_print?curator=brainpicker) and [a face mask](https://society6.com/brainpicker/collection/vintage-science-face-masks).)

We buy the plot time with the currency of our conscious choices, the grand and the mundane alike — the daily actions that make us what we are, the people who make the world what it is. Powers writes:

> Take in more, consume less, recycle everything; book-keep all hidden costs; find out where you have been set down; lobby for a smaller market; get rid of your car and travel as widely as you can (yeah, walk: what the hell); try to say a little more than you mean; carry a pocket encyclopedia (ask for one without packaging) and when the entry on “Diffusion Constant” says, “for more information, see ‘Pastry War,'” see “Pastry War.”

This latter sentiment might at first appear dated in the hindsight of two decades, in the epoch of Wikipedia. But it is actually all the more insightful and urgent today, for the quiet act of resistance at its heart has grown all the harder. What I most rue about the internet is that, for all its riches of readily accessible information, it has altered the texture of human curiosity, vanquishing that wondrous encyclopedic feeling of learning about the thing you hadn’t known you didn’t know but now greatly enjoy knowing. Somewhere along the way of choices being made for us by an insular tribe of technologists, discovery was sacrificed at the altar of search as algorithms perfected the mechanics of giving us more and more of what we already knew we wanted and believed, rendering the mind itself more and more a fixity. Would you be Googling “Pastry War” now had I not made this point about a point Richard Powers made long ago on the pages of a yellowing book I pulled from my bookshelf by some incomputable human impulse this morning?

Those choices matter, Powers reminds us, even at the smallest scale. There is no fulcrum too small for the lever of change to lift from, but the lift must begin with lucidity. He writes:

> Take a full look at the worst. Acknowledge the figures: the runaway birthdates, the irreversible extinctions and ruined habitats, the meaningless economies fueled by waste, the exported shooting wars and their cover causes… Then work at whatever comes to hand. Useful or not, it makes no difference. Jumping in is the only calculus that emergency ever allows.

Complement with Rebecca Solnit on [rewriting the world’s broken stories with our actions](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/10/18/rebecca-solnit-call-them-by-their-true-names/), then revisit [What If](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/07/29/what-if-tallec-lenain/) — a wondrous French picture-book about daring to imagine and build a different world for the children of tomorrow.

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)
